title: Third-Party Management Policy
summary: How vendors that handle company data or systems are assessed, contracted and monitored.
content_html:
Purpose

This policy protects the {{company_name}} data and systems that outside companies can reach, hold or manage for us. In this policy, a supplier is any outside company we work with in that way, such as a service provider, vendor, partner or, where it touches our systems, a customer. The policy also makes sure each supplier keeps to the security and service it agreed to.

It sets out the minimum security {{company_name}} expects from partners and other outside companies that handle {{company_name}} Confidential data.

Scope

This policy covers all data and systems that {{company_name}} owns or uses that are business critical, or that store, handle or send Confidential data. It applies to all {{company_name}} employees. It also applies to every outside party that can reach {{company_name}} data, systems or networks. That includes, among others, {{company_name}} consultants, contractors, business partners, vendors, suppliers, outsourced service providers and other outside companies.

Before a supplier gets data or access

Before a service provider can reach {{company_name}} Confidential data, systems or networks, or starts handling data for us, we check it properly.

{{company_name}} does not share or send Confidential data to a supplier until two things are in place. The first is a supplier risk assessment. The second is a signed contract, statement of work or service agreement that sets out the expected service levels and any specific security requirements.

The supplier signs up to the security rules that govern its access to our data and systems, and we keep a copy.

For each supplier, we record which regulatory or certification requirements it looks after or affects, and which ones {{company_name}} looks after itself. These can include ISO 27001, SOC 2, PCI DSS, CCPA, GDPR or other frameworks, standards and laws.

Risks that come from sharing Confidential data, or from giving a supplier access to company systems, are found, written down and dealt with as this policy describes. Managing supplier risk is part of how {{company_name}} is run, both when plans are made and in daily work. The goal is that every partnership and service meets its business aims and also meets {{company_name}} security needs.

We also look at risks that come from a supplier's own suppliers, and from the hardware, software and services the supplier relies on to serve us.

What the contract must cover

Security terms are agreed with every supplier that touches Confidential data or our systems, or that could weaken their security. The same goes for suppliers of the physical or cloud infrastructure that {{company_name}} runs on.

For suppliers that can reach {{company_name}} production systems, or could affect the security of the production environment, the written agreement includes:

  • the supplier's acceptance that it must keep company and customer data confidential
  • any commitments on the integrity, availability or privacy controls the supplier runs, so that it meets the standards {{company_name}} has set in its security program or in any relevant framework

Where the risk calls for it, the agreement also requires the supplier to manage security risks in the products and services it buys from others to deliver our service.

What we look for in a supplier's security

Every supplier must keep reasonable organizational and technical safeguards, as judged by {{company_name}}.

When we assess a supplier that receives, handles or stores Confidential data, or that can reach {{company_name}} resources, we look at the points below. Which ones apply depends on the service and on how sensitive the data is.

Their staff

The supplier's hiring and people processes include criminal background checks for every employee or contractor who can reach {{company_name}} confidential information.

Who can get into their systems

The supplier runs a technical program that controls who can get into its systems and what they can do there.

Their buildings

If the supplier stores or handles confidential data, its protections for buildings, equipment rooms and power and cooling should meet the {{company_name}} Physical Security Policy 2.

How they run their systems

The supplier follows sound, commercially reasonable practices to keep its systems running securely. These can include:

  • Technical testing
  • Protection against malicious software
  • Network protection and management
  • Finding and fixing vulnerabilities
  • Logging and monitoring
  • Incident response
  • Business continuity planning

How they build software

The supplier builds software in line with good industry practice. That includes risk assessment, formal change control, coding standards, code review and testing.

Their policies and risk program

The supplier has security policies that its senior management backs, and it reviews them regularly. It also has a program to find, judge and manage risks to its information and technology.

Laws and privacy

When we assess a supplier that will reach, store, handle or send {{company_name}} confidential data, we take into account every law and regulation that applies. The assessment should cover:

  • How customer data and company records are protected, how long records are kept, and how they are disposed of
  • How the privacy of personal information is protected

Cloud services

These rules apply when {{company_name}} uses cloud services, such as hosting, storage or software bought as a service. They set the basic limits for managing the risks that come with them.

Who is responsible:

  • The roles for choosing, using and managing cloud services are set out in the Roles and Responsibilities Policy.
  • Risks from using cloud services are managed under this policy and the Risk Management Policy.
  • Each cloud provider publishes a split of duties between itself and its customers. {{company_name}} carries out every duty that the split gives to the customer.

Before we buy:

  • The vendor security review looks at the risk of being locked in to the provider, and at how we would leave if we had to.
  • The review also looks at which security features the provider offers and how we would get and use them.

Agreements:

  • Agreements with cloud providers protect {{company_name}} data and the availability of the service, even when the provider's terms are standard and cannot be negotiated.
  • Where we can, we ask the provider to tell us in advance about major changes to how the service is delivered. Examples are changes to its technical setup, where data is stored, or which subcontractors it uses.
  • For cloud providers with a high level of built-in risk, we review the agreement every year to check it still meets our needs.

Incidents:

  • Security incidents that involve a cloud service are handled under the Incident Response Plan.

Keeping track of suppliers

{{company_name}} keeps an eye on how each supplier is doing. At least once a year, we review each supplier's security and how well it has delivered its service, and we check its work where the risk calls for it.

Suppliers sometimes change what they provide. They may change their agreements, services, technology, policies, procedures or security controls. When that happens, we look at what the change means for us. The more critical the data, systems and processes it touches, the closer we look. If the change is material, we reassess the risk and update the agreement or the way we use the service.

Exceptions

Send any request for an exception to this policy to the <role that approves exceptions to this policy, for example the CFO> for approval.

Reporting a breach of this policy

Report any known breach of this policy to the <role that receives reports of breaches of this policy, for example the CFO>. A breach can lead to system and network access being suspended or withdrawn at once. It can also lead to disciplinary action under company procedures, which can include dismissal.

2 This points to another template in this library. If you do not use it, describe the physical and environmental protections you expect here.

title: ISMS Scope Statement
summary: Sets the ISMS boundary: what is in and out and why, supplier dependencies and inherited controls, and how the management processes connect.
content_html:
Organisation: {{legal_name}}, {{registered_address}}. Owned by: {{security_lead}}.

ISMS Scope Statement

Document Type: Charter

Company Name:{{company_name}}
Document Owner:<Name and job title of the ISMS owner>Version: <Version number>
Effective Date:<Effective date>Approved By: <Name and job title of the executive sponsor>
Last Review:<Date of last review>Next Review: <Date of next review>

Purpose

This charter sets the boundary of the information security management system (ISMS) of {{company_name}}: what it covers, what it leaves out and why, which suppliers it depends on, and how the management processes connect. Leadership approves it, so staff, customers and auditors work from one agreed boundary.

Scope

This charter applies to everything named in it and to everyone who decides whether a new activity falls inside the ISMS. The risk assessment, the Statement of Applicability and every audit work from it.

Roles and Responsibilities

  • Executive sponsor (<Name and job title of the executive sponsor>): approves this charter, every exclusion and every boundary change, and accepts the risks each exclusion brings.
  • ISMS owner (<Name and job title of the ISMS owner>): maintains this charter, runs scope reviews, keeps the scope statement in Verity identical to the approved version, and informs the certification body of scope changes.
  • System and asset owners: keep their systems in Assets and tell the ISMS owner before a system or location enters or leaves the boundary.
  • Vendor owners: keep each supplier in section 4 current in Vendors and report new suppliers before they handle information in scope.
  • Internal auditor (<Name of the internal auditor or audit provider>): tests at each internal audit that the boundary in practice matches this charter, and raises any difference as a finding.

1. Scope Summary

The ISMS owner copies this paragraph word for word into the Scope statement field on the ISO 27001 Scope page in Frameworks, which prints it on the Statement of Applicability export. The two must always match.

The information security management system of {{company_name}} covers <Short description of the products and services in scope>, including the people, processes, systems and information used to build, operate and support them, from <Offices and sites in scope, or remote working only> and the hosting environments listed in this charter, in line with Statement of Applicability version <Statement of Applicability version number>.

2. What Is Inside the Boundary

  1. A product, system, location, team or supplier is inside the boundary when it stores, processes or transmits information in scope, or can change the security of something that does, such as the identity provider, the deployment pipeline and administrator devices.
  2. Each table entry below is specific enough for an auditor to tell whether an item is in or out, for example a named cloud account rather than "the cloud". Each system inside the boundary is recorded in Assets with a named owner. The ISMS owner reconciles Assets with cloud billing and identity provider records <Frequency of the asset reconciliation, for example quarterly>.
  3. Shared functions such as people operations, finance and legal are inside the boundary where they affect information in scope, for example hiring, leaving and access requests. Remote and traveling staff are inside the boundary.
  4. Where {{company_name}} also reports under SOC 2, the ISMS owner compares this boundary with the SOC 2 system description at each scope review and records any difference, with its reason, in section 3.
AreaInside the boundary
Products and services<Products and services in scope, and where each starts and ends>
Teams and functions<Teams and functions in scope, for example engineering, operations, support, security and people operations>
Offices and sites<Office addresses in scope, or None for a fully remote company>
Hosting and data centers<Cloud providers, accounts and regions in scope, and any colocation or company data centers>
Systems<Main systems in scope>. The complete list is in Assets.
Information<Types of information in scope, for example customer data, personal data, source code, keys and credentials>
Networks and endpoints<Networks and device types in scope, for example production networks and company laptops>

[Optional] For on-premises estates: list each data center, server room and disaster recovery site with its address and physical perimeter, and the network zones in scope with the firewalls or other devices that separate them. Add any colocation provider to section 4.

[Optional] For card data environments: state whether the cardholder data environment sits wholly inside this boundary. It is scoped separately and confirmed under PCI DSS requirement 12.5.2. Its system components, and the systems connected to it or able to affect its security, are recorded in Assets with PCI DSS scope set. Where segmentation keeps other systems out of PCI DSS scope, name the segmentation controls and the date of the last segmentation test. A narrower PCI DSS scope never narrows this boundary.

[Optional] For banks: state whether branches, ATMs, the core banking platform and any SWIFT environment are inside the boundary. A SWIFT environment is scoped separately for the annual SWIFT Customer Security Controls Framework attestation, in the same way as a card data environment, and a narrower SWIFT scope never narrows this boundary.

3. Exclusions

  1. An exclusion removes a part of the organization, a location, a product or a system from the boundary. Deciding that a control does not apply is different, and is recorded with its reason in the Statement of Applicability.
  2. Something the services in scope rely on for security may be excluded only if the exclusion names the controls on the interface, for example network separation that keeps production unreachable from an excluded office network.
  3. Effort or cost alone is not a reason. Valid reasons include a separate legal entity with its own security program or a product with a recorded retirement date.
Excluded itemReasonHow the interface is controlledApproved by and date
<Excluded item, or None><Reason for the exclusion><Controls at the interface, for example separate accounts and network separation><Approver and date of approval>

4. Interfaces and Dependencies

  1. The vendor owner records each supplier below in Vendors with its tier and current assurance: a SOC report in the Assurance reports section, any certificate or other report as a document on the same record.
  2. Before relying on that assurance, the vendor owner confirms it is in date and covers the service and region used, and records the controls the supplier expects its customers to run, each with an owner at {{company_name}}.
  3. Controls a supplier runs are marked in the Statement of Applicability as operated by a supplier.
  4. Interfaces with excluded parts of the organization, such as a parent company's shared IT, are listed here with the governing agreement. Duties left to customers, such as managing their own users, are stated in customer documentation.
Supplier or partyServiceControls the supplier runsControls {{company_name}} keepsAssurance and expiry
<Cloud hosting provider>Production hostingData center physical security, hardware disposal, power and coolingAccount configuration, access, encryption settings, logging, backups<Assurance report or certificate, and its expiry date>
<Other supplier or party><Service provided><Controls the supplier runs><Controls the company keeps><Assurance report or certificate, and its expiry date>

[Optional] For regulated financial institutions: reconcile this table with the register of outsourcing and third-party arrangements expected by <Name of the financial regulator>, mark each supplier that supports a critical or important function, and keep an exit plan for each as a document on its record in Vendors.

5. How the Management Processes Connect

The ISMS runs as one cycle. Each process feeds a later one and leaves a record in Verity.

ProcessOutputFeedsRecord in Verity
1. Context and interested partiesContext and Interested Parties Register2, 3, 5Documents
2. ScopeThis charter3, 4, 8Documents; Scope page in Frameworks
3. Risk assessmentRated risks with owners4Risk register
4. Risk treatmentTreatments, acceptances with expiry, Statement of Applicability5, 6Risk register; Applicability page in Frameworks
5. Objectives and planningInformation Security Objectives and Plan6, 7Documents; Tasks
6. Control operationEvidence, approved documents, completed tasks7, 8Evidence; Documents; Tasks
7. Monitoring and measurementSecurity performance report9Evidence on control GOV-26
8. Internal auditAudit report and findings9, 10Evidence on control GOV-13; Tasks
9. Management reviewDecisions and actionsAllEvidence on control GOV-15; Tasks
10. Corrective action and improvementActions closed with evidence1, 3, 5Tasks; improvement log as evidence on control GOV-30
11. Operating planRecurring security activities with owners and schedules6, 7Recurring tasks in Tasks; evidence on control GOV-29
12. Support: competence, awareness, communication and document controlCompetence records, training and acknowledgement records, controlled documents6, 8Documents (approvals, versions, acknowledgement campaigns); evidence on controls HR-09 and GOV-28

6. Approval, Communication and Change

  1. Each version is approved through the approval tiers in Documents, with the executive sponsor as final approver, before publication.
  2. After publication, the ISMS owner runs an acknowledgement campaign in Documents for <Roles who must acknowledge the scope, for example control owners and team leads>, due within <Number of days allowed to acknowledge> days.
  3. The scope summary may be shared externally. The full charter is internal and is shared outside {{company_name}} only under a confidentiality agreement.
  4. These events trigger a scope review before the change goes live: a new product or service; a new office, data center or cloud region; an acquisition or divestment; a new supplier running part of a service in scope; a contract or regulation naming a service; closing a site.
  5. The owner of the change raises a task in Tasks for the ISMS owner, who records the outcome within <Number of business days to assess a scope change> business days and updates the risk assessment and Statement of Applicability if the boundary moves.
  6. At each review the ISMS owner checks the boundary against the Context and Interested Parties Register: every service a contract or regulator expects the ISMS to cover is inside it, and each internal or external issue that bears on what the ISMS should cover, such as a new market, an acquisition or a change of hosting, is reflected in the boundary or in a recorded exclusion reason. The review task lists the CTX and IP rows considered.
  7. Where {{company_name}} holds a certificate, the ISMS owner informs the certification body of a scope change within the period its agreement sets, and always before the next audit.

Records and Evidence

RecordWhere it is kept in VerityRetention
Approved charter, every version, including the process mapDocuments, with version history and approvals; each approved version attached as evidence to control GOV-23<Retention period for ISMS records, for example three years after the record is superseded>
Scope summaryISO 27001 Scope page in Frameworks; each Statement of Applicability export attached as evidence to control GOV-27As above
Scope reviews and change assessmentsA task in Tasks with owner, due date and outcome; review notes attached as evidence to control GOV-23As above
Supplier assurance and customer controlsThe supplier's record in VendorsAs above, counted from contract end

Exceptions

A temporary gap between this charter and practice, such as an acquired business not yet inside the boundary, is allowed only when it is in the Risk register with an owner and treatment, any acceptance expires within <Maximum length of a scope exception, for example six months>, the executive sponsor approves it, and it is reported at the next management review.

Review

The ISMS owner reviews this charter at least once a year, before the management review and each certification or surveillance audit, and after any trigger in section 6. Reviews that change nothing are still recorded.

Related Documents

  • Information Security Policy
  • Information Security Roles and Responsibilities Policy
  • Context and Interested Parties Register
  • Information Security Objectives and Plan
  • Risk Management Policy
  • Asset Management Policy
  • Third-Party Management Policy
  • Statement of Applicability (exported from Frameworks)

title: Context and Interested Parties Register
summary: Register of internal and external issues, interested parties and their requirements, and the compliance obligations register, with owners and reviews.
content_html:
Context and Interested Parties Register

Document Type: Standard

Company Name:{{company_name}}
Document Owner:<Name and job title of the ISMS owner>Version: <Version number>
Effective Date:<Effective date>Approved By: <Name and job title of the executive sponsor>
Last Review:<Date of last review>Next Review: <Date of next review>

Purpose

This register records the issues inside and outside {{company_name}} that shape what the security program has to deal with, and the parties who have a stake in it with what each one requires. It shows which requirements the program takes on, who owns each entry, and where each entry led: a risk, an objective, a scope decision, a control or a recorded decision to take no action.

Scope

The register covers the information security management system (ISMS) defined in the ISMS Scope Statement. Section 6 is the compliance obligations register. The register is an input to the scope, the risk assessment and the security objectives, and applies to everyone named as an owner in it.

Roles and Responsibilities

  • ISMS owner (<Name and job title of the ISMS owner>): maintains the register, collects input before each review, and records where each entry led.
  • Executive sponsor (<Name and job title of the executive sponsor>): approves the register and every decision not to address a legal, regulatory or contractual requirement.
  • Obligations owner (<Name and job title of the owner of the compliance obligations register>): keeps section 6 current and maps each legal, regulatory and contractual requirement to the controls that meet it.
  • Relationship owners: keep the rows for the parties they manage current, as named in the Owner column, for example customer success for customers, legal for regulators, people operations for staff and procurement for suppliers.
  • Risk owners: assess risks raised from entries in this register.

1. Maintaining the Register

  1. Before each review the ISMS owner gathers input from: the business plan and leadership minutes; customer contracts, security questionnaires and deals lost on security grounds; legal and regulatory updates; incidents; internal and external audit findings; supplier changes recorded in Vendors; and threat reports reviewed under control LM-12.
  2. Issues are numbered CTX-nn and interested parties IP-nn. Each row has an owner and the date it was last reviewed, and the owner updates that date at each review.
  3. For each issue the owner records its effect on the security program and the response, naming the record it led to: a risk in the Risk register, an objective in the Information Security Objectives and Plan, a change to the ISMS Scope Statement, a control or document change, or no action with the reason.
  4. Rows that no longer apply are marked closed with the date and reason, never deleted, so the history stays visible.
  5. The register states whether climate change is a relevant issue for the security program and why, including when the answer is no. ISO/IEC 27001:2022/Amd 1:2024 added this point to clause 4.1 and a related note to clause 4.2.

2. Issues

The rows below are common starting points. Keep, change or close each one, and add issues specific to {{company_name}}.

IDIssueTypeEffect on the security programResponse and recordOwnerReviewed
CTX-01Customers ask for independent assurance before buying and renewingExternalSales depend on audit reports and timely questionnaire answersObjective and scope: <Reference to the risk, objective or record><Owner><Review date>
CTX-02Data protection and security laws in the markets served: <Main laws and regulations that apply>ExternalLegal duties on breach notice, transfers and retentionSection 6 and risks: <Reference to the risk, objective or record><Owner><Review date>
CTX-03Threats such as ransomware, credential theft and attacks through software dependenciesExternalSets priorities for identity, backup and dependency controlsRisks: <Reference to the risk, objective or record><Owner><Review date>
CTX-04Reliance on cloud and software-as-a-service suppliersExternalAvailability and data protection depend on supplier controlsRisks and supplier reviews: <Reference to the risk, objective or record><Owner><Review date>
CTX-05Climate change and severe weatherExternal<Whether climate change is relevant to the security program, and why><Risk reference, or no action with the reason><Owner><Review date>
CTX-06Growth in staff, products and marketsInternalAccess and scope change faster than reviewsScope review trigger and objective: <Reference to the risk, objective or record><Owner><Review date>
CTX-07Size and skills of the security teamInternalLimits how much can be done by hand; drives automation and hiringObjective with resources: <Reference to the risk, objective or record><Owner><Review date>
CTX-08Technology choices, including staff use of AI toolsInternalNew data flows and new suppliersRisks: <Reference to the risk, objective or record><Owner><Review date>
CTX-09Security culture and awarenessInternalPhishing and data handling mistakesObjective: <Reference to the risk, objective or record><Owner><Review date>
CTX-10Budget and funding cycleInternalSets when security investment can happenManagement review decision: <Reference to the risk, objective or record><Owner><Review date>

[Optional] For on-premises estates: add issues such as hardware and operating system end of life, data center power and cooling capacity, physical hazards at each site, and reliance on a few people who know older systems.

3. Interested Parties

Requirement types are legal (law or regulation), contractual (a signed agreement) or other (an expectation with no legal or contract basis). Keep, change or close each starter row.

IDPartyWhat they requireTypeAddressedHowOwnerReviewed
IP-01CustomersProtection and availability of their data, notice of incidents that affect them, evidence of controls, security terms and data processing agreementsContractualYesControls, contracts, assurance reports<Owner><Review date>
IP-02Regulators and data protection authorities: <Regulators that oversee the company>Lawful processing, breach notice within legal deadlines, cooperation with inquiriesLegalYesSection 6, Incident Response Plan<Owner><Review date>
IP-03Employees and contractorsClear rules, training, protection of their personal data, a safe way to raise concernsLegal and otherYesPolicies, training, people processes<Owner><Review date>
IP-04Suppliers and cloud providersCustomers run the controls their service relies on, and follow acceptable use termsContractualYesISMS Scope Statement section 4, Vendors<Owner><Review date>
IP-05Owners, board and investorsSecurity risk reported and kept within appetiteOther<Yes, Partly or No, with the reason>Management review, risk reporting<Owner><Review date>
IP-06Cyber insurerMinimum controls for cover, such as multi-factor authentication and offline backupsContractualYesControls, renewal questionnaire<Owner><Review date>
IP-07Certification body and auditorsAccess to records and people, an accurate scope, notice of significant changesContractualYesDocuments, Evidence, Statement of Applicability<Owner><Review date>
IP-08People whose personal data is processedData used only as described, kept secure, rights honoredLegalYesData Management Policy, section 6<Owner><Review date>

[Optional] For regulated financial institutions: add the prudential and conduct supervisors, the central bank, payment schemes and any deposit or investor protection body, with their expectations on operational resilience, outsourcing, data residency and localization, incident reporting and testing. Record supervisory findings and the board-approved risk appetite as issues, and enter each supervisory finding in section 6 with its deadline.

[Optional] For card data environments: add the acquiring bank, the card brands and payment service providers as interested parties. The acquirer's requirement to validate against PCI DSS, and the validation method it accepts, is a contractual requirement for section 6. Where {{company_name}} stores, processes or transmits card data for other businesses, or can affect the security of their card data, add those customers as an interested party. Their requirement for a current Attestation of Compliance and a written split of PCI DSS responsibilities is a contractual requirement for section 6.

4. Deciding What the Program Addresses

  1. Legal, regulatory and contractual requirements are addressed by default. Not addressing one needs the executive sponsor's written approval, a reason, and a risk in the Risk register.
  2. For other expectations, the ISMS owner and the relationship owner decide, and the reason is written in the Addressed column.
  3. Within <Number of business days to update the obligations register> business days of a row being added or changed, the obligations owner records each legal, regulatory and contractual requirement in section 6 with its source, owner, review date and the controls that meet it.
  4. Security commitments in individual contracts that go beyond the standard terms are recorded in section 6 against the customer, so they survive staff changes.
  5. Conflicting requirements, such as a customer retention demand against a legal deletion duty, go to <Role that resolves conflicting requirements, for example General Counsel>, and the decision is recorded on both rows.

5. Review and Reporting

  1. The ISMS owner reviews the whole register at least once a year, before the management review, and each relationship owner confirms their rows.
  2. These events trigger an earlier review of the affected rows: a funding round, acquisition or new market; a new regulator or law that applies; a major contract with new security terms; a serious incident; a major supplier change; or a significant new threat to the technology in use.
  3. Each review is a task in Tasks with the ISMS owner and a due date. Risks raised are entered in the Risk register before the task is closed.
  4. Changes since the last review are summarized as an input to management review under ISO/IEC 27001 clause 9.3.2.

6. Legal, Regulatory and Contractual Requirements

This section is the compliance obligations register. Each legal, regulatory and contractual requirement found through sections 3 and 4 has its own row, specific enough to check: the law and the articles that apply, the regulation and rule, or the contract and clause. Terms in the standard customer contract are recorded once. Terms agreed with one customer are recorded against that customer.

IDRequirement and sourcePartyWhat it requires of the security programControls and documents that meet itOwnerStatusReviewed
OBL-01<Data protection law, with the articles that apply>IP-02, IP-08<For example security of processing, breach notice to the authority within the legal deadline, records of processing><Control codes and documents, for example DM-01 and the Incident Response Plan><Owner><Met, Partly met or Not met, with the risk reference if not fully met><Review date>
OBL-02Standard customer terms and data processing agreement, version <Version of the standard terms>IP-01<For example security commitments, breach notice period, subprocessor notice, audit rights><Control codes and documents><Owner><Status><Review date>
OBL-03<Laws that set how long records must or may be kept, for example tax, employment and financial records>IP-02Minimum and maximum retention for the records named<Control codes and documents, for example DM-08><Owner><Status><Review date>
OBL-04<Laws on the use, import or export of encryption in the countries where {{company_name}} operates, or None>IP-02<Restrictions or licenses that apply><Control codes and documents, for example the Cryptography Policy><Owner><Status><Review date>

The obligations owner checks for new or changed laws and regulations <Frequency of the legal update check, for example quarterly> through <Source of legal and regulatory updates, for example outside counsel or a regulatory update service>, and records each check as a task in Tasks, including checks that find nothing.

Records and Evidence

RecordWhere it is kept in VerityRetention
Approved register, every versionDocuments, with version history and approvals; each approved version attached as evidence to controls GOV-24 and GOV-25<Retention period for ISMS records, for example three years after the record is superseded>
Review recordsA task in Tasks with owner, due date and outcome; review notes attached as evidence to controls GOV-24 and GOV-25As above
Compliance obligations register (section 6) and legal update checksDocuments, as part of this register, with each approved version attached as evidence to control GOV-05; update checks as tasks in TasksAs above
Risks raised from the registerRisk register, with the CTX or IP number in the risk descriptionAs above, counted from risk closure
Decisions not to address a requirementApproval in Documents and the related risk in the Risk register, with any acceptance expiry dateAs above

Exceptions

A legal, regulatory or contractual requirement that cannot be met by its due date is recorded as a risk with an owner and a treatment. Any acceptance needs the executive sponsor's approval and an expiry date no more than <Maximum length of a risk acceptance for an unmet requirement, for example twelve months> away, and is reported at the next management review.

Review

This register is reviewed at least once a year and after any trigger in section 5. Reviews that change nothing are still recorded.

title: Information Security Objectives and Plan
summary: Measurable security objectives with owners, targets and dates, program-wide resources, and the plan for measuring and reviewing performance.
content_html:
Information Security Objectives and Plan

Document Type: Standard

Company Name:{{company_name}}
Document Owner:<Name and job title of the ISMS owner>Version: <Version number>
Effective Date:<Effective date>Approved By: <Name and job title of the executive sponsor>
Last Review:<Date of last review>Next Review: <Date of next review>

Purpose

This standard sets the information security objectives of {{company_name}}, the plan and resources to reach each one, and how progress and the performance of the security program are measured, analyzed and judged. It lets leadership check whether security work is succeeding and whether the people and budget behind it are enough.

Scope

It covers the information security management system (ISMS) defined in the ISMS Scope Statement, for the period <Objectives period, for example the fiscal year>, and applies to everyone named as an owner in it.

Roles and Responsibilities

  • Executive sponsor (<Name and job title of the executive sponsor>): approves objectives, targets and resources, and decides on results at management review.
  • ISMS owner (<Name and job title of the ISMS owner>): drafts the objectives, maintains this plan, defines the measures, and compiles and analyzes the results.
  • Budget holder (<Name and job title of the budget holder>): confirms funding for each objective and for the program resources in section 6 before approval.
  • Objective owners: deliver the plan for their objective and update its status <Frequency of status updates, for example monthly>.
  • Measure owners: collect each measure as defined, on schedule, from the named source.
  • Internal auditor: traces a sample of reported results back to source data at each internal audit.

1. Setting Objectives

  1. The ISMS owner drafts the objectives once a year, before the objectives period starts.
  2. Each objective names its source: a commitment in the Information Security Policy, a risk in the Risk register, a requirement in the Context and Interested Parties Register, or a finding from an audit or management review.
  3. The ISMS owner checks each objective against the Information Security Policy and records the policy commitment it serves. An objective that conflicts with the policy, or cannot be traced to it, is rewritten or dropped.
  4. Each objective has a measure and a numeric target where one is practical. Where it is not, the table states the evidence that will show the objective was achieved.
  5. There are between three and eight objectives, so each one gets real attention.
  6. The executive sponsor approves the objectives and their resources together, through the approval tiers in Documents.
  7. After publication, the ISMS owner runs an acknowledgement campaign in Documents for objective owners and measure owners, and summarizes the objectives for all staff through <Channel for staff security communications>.

2. Objectives

The rows below are common starting points. Keep, change or delete each one. Status is one of: Not started, On track, At risk, Off track, Achieved, Not achieved, Withdrawn.

IDObjective and sourceMeasureTargetOwnerResourcesDueHow evaluatedStatus
OBJ-01Fix serious weaknesses quickly. Source: <Policy commitment or risk reference>Critical and high findings in Vulnerabilities closed within SLA, as a share of those due in the quarter<Target, for example 95 percent><Objective owner><People, time and budget needed><Due date>Quarterly result against targetNot started
OBJ-02Keep access limited to need. Source: <Policy commitment or risk reference>Access reviews completed on time, with every removal done, as a share of those scheduled<Target, for example 95 percent><Objective owner><People, time and budget needed><Due date>Quarterly result against targetNot started
OBJ-03Build security awareness. Source: <Policy commitment or risk reference>Staff who completed training by their due date; share of simulated phishing emails reported<Target, for example 95 percent><Objective owner><People, time and budget needed><Due date>Quarterly result and trendNot started
OBJ-04Know the security of key suppliers. Source: <Policy commitment or risk reference>Highest-tier suppliers in Vendors with an assurance review in the last twelve months<Target, for example 95 percent><Objective owner><People, time and budget needed><Due date>Quarterly result against targetNot started
OBJ-05Prove that recovery works. Source: <Policy commitment or risk reference>Critical systems restored in a test within their recovery time and recovery point targets<Target, for example every critical system once a year><Objective owner><People, time and budget needed><Due date>Test reports against targetsNot started
OBJ-06Close audit findings on time. Source: <Policy commitment or risk reference>Audit findings and corrective actions in Tasks closed by their due date<Target, for example 95 percent><Objective owner><People, time and budget needed><Due date>Quarterly result against targetNot started

3. Plan and Tracking

  1. Within one month of approval, each objective owner creates a task in Tasks for the objective, with sub-tasks for the main actions, each with an owner and a due date.
  2. Each measure collected on a schedule is set up as a recurring task for its measure owner.
  3. An objective is At risk when it is forecast to miss its target or date, and Off track when it has missed a checkpoint. Off track for two updates in a row is escalated to the executive sponsor and listed for the next management review.
  4. Changing a target, due date or owner needs the executive sponsor's approval and a new version of this document.
  5. An objective Not achieved by its due date gets a corrective action task with the cause and the fix, recorded in the improvement log under control GOV-30.

4. Monitoring and Measurement Plan

  1. Each measure has a written definition: what is counted, the source, the period and the formula, so results from different periods can be compared. When a definition changes, the change is recorded and earlier results are restated or marked as not comparable.
  2. Data is taken from the system of record and each extract is saved with its date. Results are never typed in from memory.
  3. Where team size allows, the person who analyzes a measure is not the person whose work it measures.
  4. A result is green on target, amber when within <Tolerance before a measure turns red, for example 10 percentage points> of target, and red beyond that.
What is measuredMethod and sourceMeasured byCollectedAnalyzed byReviewed by
Objectives OBJ-01 to OBJ-06As defined in section 2Objective owners<Measurement frequency, for example monthly>ISMS owner, quarterlyManagement review
Control status and evidence coverageISO 27001 dashboard in Frameworks<Measure owner>MonthlyISMS owner, quarterlyManagement review
Control effectivenessFailing automated checks per control, from the Checks tab on each control page, and controls found not operating in internal audit tests, from the internal audit report<Measure owner>MonthlyISMS owner, quarterlyManagement review
Risk treatmentRisk register: treatments past due date, acceptances past expiry<Measure owner>MonthlyISMS owner, quarterlyManagement review
Overdue workTasks: open items past due date, by severity<Measure owner>MonthlyISMS owner, quarterlyManagement review
Document upkeepDocuments: items past review date; acknowledgement completion<Measure owner>QuarterlyISMS owner, quarterlyManagement review
Security incidentsCount by severity and time to contain, from <Incident tracking tool><Measure owner>MonthlyISMS owner, quarterlyManagement review

[Optional] For on-premises estates: add patch currency by server class, systems past vendor end of support, backup success for on-premises systems and completion of physical access reviews.

[Optional] For card data environments: add measures for the PCI DSS activities that run on a schedule, such as scan results under requirements 11.3.1 and 11.3.2, log review under requirement 10.4.1 and targeted risk analyses under requirement 12.3.1, and keep them as evidence for the PCI DSS assessment.

5. Analysis, Evaluation and Resources

  1. Each quarter the ISMS owner writes a security performance report: results against targets, the trend over at least the last four periods, the cause of each red result, and a conclusion on whether the ISMS is meeting its objectives.
  2. The report is presented at the management review. For each objective the review records one decision, with an owner: continue, change resources, change target or date, or withdraw.
  3. The Resources column states people, time, tools and budget. A shortfall that puts an objective at risk is raised at the next management review and, if not resolved there, recorded as a risk in the Risk register.

[Optional] For regulated financial institutions: align these measures and thresholds with the key risk indicators and risk appetite in the operational risk framework, and report results to the board risk committee <Board reporting frequency, for example quarterly>.

6. Resources for the Security Program

Once a year, before the objectives period starts, the ISMS owner sets out the resources the whole security program needs, not only those tied to an objective. The budget holder confirms what is provided, and the executive sponsor approves this table with the objectives. A gap that is not closed is decided at the next management review and, if it is left open, recorded as a risk in the Risk register.

ResourceNeeded for the periodProvidedGap and decision
People in security roles, in full-time equivalents<Number needed><Number provided><Gap and decision, or None>
Security tools and services<Tools and services needed><Tools and services provided><Gap and decision, or None>
External support, such as internal audit, penetration testing and the certification body<Support needed><Support contracted><Gap and decision, or None>
Training for people in security roles<Training needed><Training funded><Gap and decision, or None>
Budget for the period<Amount requested><Amount approved><Gap and decision, or None>

Records and Evidence

RecordWhere it is kept in VerityRetention
Approved objectives and plan, every versionDocuments, with version history and approvals; each approved version attached as evidence to control GOV-26<Retention period for ISMS records, for example three years after the record is superseded>
Program resource table and budget holder confirmationThis document, each approved version attached as evidence to control GOV-26; resourcing decisions in the management review minutes on control GOV-15As above
Plan tasks, recurring measure tasks and status historyTasksAs above
Measure definitions, data extracts and quarterly reportAttached as evidence to control GOV-26 each quarterAs above
Management review decisions on objectives and resourcesMinutes attached as evidence to control GOV-15; actions as tasks in TasksAs above
Corrective actions for missed objectivesTasksAs above

Exceptions

A measure that cannot be produced for a period, for example because a source system was unavailable, is reported as a gap with the reason, never estimated. A gap in two periods in a row gets a corrective action task. An objective is withdrawn during the period only with the executive sponsor's approval and a recorded reason.

Review

The ISMS owner reviews this document once a year before the objectives period starts and at each management review, and earlier after a scope change, a major change in risk, a serious incident, a reorganization, a budget change or an audit finding about objectives.

Related Documents

  • Information Security Policy
  • ISMS Scope Statement
  • Context and Interested Parties Register
  • Risk Management Policy
  • Information Security Roles and Responsibilities Policy
  • Incident Response Plan
  • Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery (BC/DR)

title: Risk Assessment and Treatment Methodology
summary: How risks are identified, scored against appetite and treated, and how controls, the Statement of Applicability and residual risk are approved.
content_html:
Risk Assessment and Treatment Methodology

Document Type: Procedure

Company Name:{{company_name}}
Document Owner:<Name and job title of the document owner>Version: <Version number>
Effective Date:<Date>Approved By: <Name and job title of the approver>
Last Review:<Date>Next Review: <Date>

Purpose

This procedure sets out how {{company_name}} identifies, analyzes, evaluates and treats information security risks, using the same rules every time so one cycle can be set against the next, and how controls, the Statement of Applicability and residual risk are approved. It puts the Risk Management Policy into practice and supports ISO/IEC 27001 clauses 6.1.1, 6.1.2, 6.1.3, 8.2 and 8.3.

Scope

All information, systems, services, people, sites and suppliers inside the scope of the {{company_name}} information security management system (ISMS), the risks and opportunities for the ISMS itself, and the opportunities to improve security found while assessing them.

Roles and Responsibilities

  • Risk Manager (<Name and job title of the risk manager>): owns this procedure and the risk register settings in Verity, runs each assessment, maintains the Statement of Applicability and reports to management review.
  • Risk owners: named individuals with the authority and budget to act on a risk. They agree ratings, approve treatment and accept residual risk within the limits in section 4.
  • Control owners: operate selected controls and complete the treatment tasks assigned to them.
  • Top management (<Name of the leadership body, for example the executive team>): approves appetite and tolerance, the annual report and the Statement of Applicability, and decides on risks above appetite.

Procedure

1. Inputs and identification

  1. The Risk Manager gathers the ISMS scope, the registers of issues, interested parties and obligations, Verity Assets, Vendors and Vulnerabilities, recent incidents and audit findings, and threat intelligence, and lists each input in the report.
  2. For each in-scope service, process and critical supplier, the Risk Manager and service owner describe scenarios: the threat, the weakness exploited, the assets affected and the consequence for confidentiality, integrity or availability.
  3. Every assessment explicitly covers fraud and insider misuse (including management override), supplier failure, legal and contractual breach and planned changes, and records the fraud conclusion even when low.
  4. Each risk is entered in the Verity risk register with a description, category, linked assets or vendors and one named risk owner, who is a person and never a team. Improvement opportunities are raised as tasks in Verity Tasks with an owner and due date.
  5. The assessment also records risks and opportunities for the ISMS itself, such as loss of a key person, a budget cut, weak management support or a new customer requirement, drawn from the issues and interested parties registers. They are treated in the same register.

2. Analysis scale

This table matches the five-level scale configured in the Verity risk register and changes whenever those settings change.

LevelLikelihoodImpact
1Rare: not expected within five yearsNegligible: no customer effect, no data exposed
2Unlikely: once in two to five yearsMinor: brief degradation within service levels, limited internal data exposed
3Possible: once in one to two yearsModerate: service levels missed for some customers, or confidential data of a few customers or staff exposed
4Likely: at least once a yearMajor: extended core outage, or a breach needing regulator or customer notification
5Almost certain: several times a yearSevere: threatens the business or leads to regulatory action

Financial thresholds per impact level: <Financial loss bands for impact levels 1 to 5, in your currency>. Where descriptions point to different levels, the highest applies.

3. Risk analysis

  1. The assessor rates inherent likelihood and impact as if the controls specific to the risk were absent, then residual likelihood and impact using only controls that operate today, as shown by their status and evidence in Verity. Planned controls do not lower the residual rating.
  2. Verity scores each rating with the formula in the register settings (<Scoring formula, for example likelihood multiplied by impact>) and places it in the configured bands (<Score bands, for example 1 to 4 Low, 5 to 9 Medium, 10 to 16 High, 20 to 25 Critical>).
  3. A short rationale is written on each risk so another assessor would reach the same rating.
  4. All risks in a cycle use the same scale, formula and bands. Changing them is a revision of this procedure, after which the Risk Manager re-scores every open risk.

4. Evaluation and acceptance criteria

  1. Appetite and tolerance are set per top-level category in the register settings and approved by top management each year: appetite <Risk appetite per category, for example residual score up to 9>, tolerance <Risk tolerance per category, for example residual score up to 16>.
  2. Residual scores are compared with their category's appetite, and treatment is prioritized by residual score.
  3. Every risk has its residual risk accepted, including risks within appetite that need no further treatment. Each acceptance is recorded on the risk in Verity with a rationale and an expiry date, within the limits below. Verity records one requester and one approver and does not let anyone approve their own request. Within appetite, the Risk Manager requests the acceptance and names the risk owner as approver. Above appetite, the risk owner requests it and names the role in the table as approver, so the request and the approval together show that both agreed. Approvers need the Verity permission to approve risks. Verity does not check the approver against this table, so each quarter the Risk Manager confirms that every active acceptance was approved at the right level and reports any that were not to management review. When an acceptance expires, Verity reopens the risk and the owner decides again.
Residual positionWho may acceptLongest period
Within appetiteRisk owner<Maximum acceptance period within appetite, for example 12 months>
Above appetite, within toleranceRisk owner and <Role that accepts risks above appetite, for example the CEO><Maximum acceptance period above appetite, for example 6 months>
Above toleranceNot accepted: treat it or stop the activity. Only <Body that may grant an exception above tolerance, for example the board> may grant a time-limited exception. Its minutes are linked to the risk as evidence, and the acceptance in Verity names <Person who records exceptions for that body, for example the board chair> as approver.<Maximum exception period, for example 3 months>

5. Treatment and control selection

  1. For every risk above appetite the risk owner records one or more options on the risk: mitigate (add or strengthen controls), avoid (stop or change the activity), transfer (insurance or contract, with the owner still accountable for what remains) or accept under section 4.
  2. To mitigate, the risk owner and Risk Manager select controls from the Verity control library, link them to the risk and record the expected residual rating in the risk's treatment plan field. The residual likelihood and impact fields keep the current position until the treatment is in place (section 3.1).
  3. Controls are chosen from the risk. The Risk Manager then cross-checks the selection against the Annex A list in the Verity ISO 27001 framework and confirms, for each Annex A control not selected, that no risk, obligation or scope reason needs it. Gaps go into the treatment plan.
  4. Risks with no linked control or acceptance, and controls linked to no risk or obligation, are resolved before the annual report is approved.

6. Statement of Applicability

  1. The Risk Manager maintains the Statement of Applicability in Verity Frameworks, recording for every Annex A control the decision (applicable or excluded), the reason for including or excluding it, and the owner. Verity shows whether each applicable control is implemented from the status of the controls linked to it. Where a control is not yet implemented, the reason names the treatment task that will implement it.
  2. Each reason names a risk, a legal, regulatory or contractual obligation, or the ISMS scope. "Not relevant" and "best practice" are not reasons.
  3. Controls a supplier operates for {{company_name}} are marked applicable with Operated by set to supplier and the supplier named in the reason, and the supplier's assurance report is kept on its record in Verity Vendors.
  4. The Risk Manager exports the Statement, with the ISMS scope statement at the top, to XLSX, risk owners confirm decisions on their risks, and the export is attached as evidence to control GOV-27. <Name and job title of the Statement of Applicability approver> approves it by approving that evidence item in Verity, which records who approved it and when.
  5. The Statement is reissued when the treatment plan, scope or an Annex A decision changes, and at least once per cycle.

7. Treatment plan and residual risk

  1. The risk treatment plan is the set of tasks in Verity Tasks linked to each risk, each with an owner, a due date and a severity matching the risk band. Due dates follow <Treatment deadlines by band, for example Critical 30 days, High 90 days, Medium 180 days>.
  2. The risk owner approves the plan under their own Verity account by marking the risk reviewed with a note that approves the treatment decision and plan. The risk history and audit log then show the risk owner as the approver, with the date. An entry made by someone else on the owner's behalf is not the owner's approval.
  3. A task closes only when evidence of the action is linked to it or attached to the related control. Only then is the residual rating lowered, and the owner accepts the result (with an expiry date) or adds treatment.
  4. Overdue tasks are reported at every management review. Tasks overdue by more than <Number of days overdue before escalation> days go to top management.
  5. At each register review, at the cadence set in the Verity register settings (which gives each open risk its next review date), the risk owner checks that the linked controls still operate, using their current evidence and check results in Verity, and that the risk has not occurred again. The owner records the result by marking the risk reviewed with a note. A treatment that did not work goes back to section 5.

8. Intervals and triggers

  1. A full assessment is completed at least annually, by <Month by which the annual assessment is completed>, and the register is reviewed at each management review, <Frequency of risk register reviews, for example quarterly>.
  2. A targeted assessment of the affected risks, following sections 1 to 7, is completed before go-live, or within <Number of business days after an unplanned event> business days of an unplanned event, for: a new product handling customer data; a hosting, region or major architecture change; a new supplier with access to customer data; a new data type, jurisdiction or regulation; a reorganization; a major incident or audit finding; or an actively exploited vulnerability in scope.
  3. The Risk Manager writes an annual report of scope, inputs, risks by band, acceptances and treatment status. The report is attached as evidence to control GOV-18. Top management's approval is recorded by <Name and job title of the person who approves for top management> approving that evidence item in Verity, or by attaching the signed minutes of the meeting that approved it.

[Optional] For regulated financial institutions: align categories and the impact scale with the operational risk framework and <Name of the financial regulator> expectations, have the second line risk function challenge the assessment, report risks above appetite to <Name of the board risk committee>, and assess outsourcing and concentration risk.

[Optional] For an on-premises estate: add data centers, power, network equipment and end-of-life systems to the inputs, and confirm every site has an assessed risk.

[Optional] For a card data environment: keep with this assessment the targeted risk analyses for PCI DSS v4.0.1 requirement 12.3.1, and for 12.3.2 for any requirement met with the customized approach, and review each at least every 12 months and when the environment changes. Keep the yearly review of cryptographic cipher suites and protocols (12.3.3) and of hardware and software technologies (12.3.4) with it, and use the confirmed card data environment scope as an input.

Records and Evidence

Records are retained for <Retention period for risk records, for example three years after they are superseded>, and approved Statements of Applicability for as long as the ISMS operates.

RecordWhere it is kept in Verity
Risks, ratings, owners, treatment decisions, risk-to-control links, acceptances and reviewsRisk register, with every change in the audit log (controls GOV-19 and GOV-07)
Quarterly check that acceptances were approved at the right levelEvidence attached to control GOV-19
Annual report and its approval; fraud analysis; targeted assessmentsEvidence attached to controls GOV-18, GOV-12 and GOV-03
Statement of Applicability versions and approvalsFrameworks, with approved XLSX exports attached as evidence to control GOV-27
Treatment plan and completionTasks linked to each risk, with a quarterly status summary attached as evidence to control GOV-20

Exceptions

A departure from this procedure is approved in advance by <Role that approves exceptions to this procedure>, recorded as a risk with an acceptance and expiry date, and reported at the next management review.

Review

The Risk Manager reviews this procedure at least annually, against its review date in Verity Documents, and earlier when the scale, formula, appetite or ISMS scope change, or after a major incident or an audit finding on risk management.

Related Documents

  • Risk Management Policy
  • Information Security Policy
  • Asset Management Policy
  • Third-Party Management Policy
  • Change Management Procedure
  • Document and Record Control Procedure

title: Change Management Procedure
summary: How production and ISMS changes are classified, reviewed, tested, approved, released, rolled back and reviewed, including emergency changes.
content_html:
Change Management Procedure

Document Type: Procedure

Company Name:{{company_name}}
Document Owner:<Name and job title of the document owner>Version: <Version number>
Effective Date:<Date>Approved By: <Name and job title of the approver>
Last Review:<Date>Next Review: <Date>

Purpose

This procedure sets out how {{company_name}} requests, assesses, approves, tests, releases and reviews changes to production systems and to its information security management system (ISMS), so that every change is authorized, traceable and reversible. It supports ISO/IEC 27001 control A.8.32, with A.8.9, A.8.31 and clause 6.3, and SOC 2 criterion CC8.1.

Scope

  • Changes to production: application code, infrastructure as code, data migrations, cloud, network, identity, encryption and logging settings, and the configuration of third-party services that hold customer data.
  • Baseline configurations of servers, containers, endpoints and network devices.
  • Changes to the ISMS itself, such as its scope, roles, risk method or key suppliers.
  • Out of scope: work that never leaves a developer's own environment. Edits to controlled documents follow the Document and Record Control Procedure.

Roles and Responsibilities

  • Change requester: raises the change record and states the reason.
  • Implementer: builds, tests, releases and verifies the change and owns its rollback.
  • Peer reviewer: a qualified person other than the author who reviews the code or configuration.
  • Change approver: <Default change approver, for example the engineering manager who owns the service>.
  • Change Advisory Board (CAB): <Members of the change advisory board, for example the CTO, the security lead and the head of support>. Meets <CAB meeting frequency, for example weekly> and on demand.
  • Emergency change authorizer: <Roles allowed to authorize an emergency change, for example the on-call engineering lead or the CTO>.
  • Baseline owner: <Name and job title of the baseline owner>, who maintains the configuration baselines and their approved deviations.
  • Procedure owner: maintains this procedure, runs the quarterly sample and reports to management review.

Procedure

1. Change categories and risk rating

CategoryWhen it appliesApproval before release
StandardLow risk, repeatable, listed in the standard change catalog kept in Verity Documents, for example dependency patches that pass all checks or automated certificate renewalPre-approved by the CAB when added to the catalog; each use is still recorded, and code changes are peer reviewed
Normal, low riskInternal or reversible with no effect on security controls or customer dataPeer review approval
Normal, medium riskVisible to customers, or infrastructure change with a tested rollbackPeer review and change approver
Normal, high riskAny change meeting a high-risk criterion belowPeer review, change approver and CAB
EmergencyNeeded at once to restore service or contain an active incident or exploited vulnerabilityEmergency change authorizer, then retrospective approval (section 4)

A change is high risk if it alters authentication, authorization, encryption, logging or the network boundary; changes how customer or personal data is stored or moved; includes a data migration that cannot be reversed; has no tested rollback; or touches <Systems that always need CAB approval, for example the payments service and the production database>. The change approver can raise a rating.

2. Normal change steps

  1. Request. The requester opens a change record in <Name of the change tracking tool, for example Jira or GitHub Issues> stating the description, reason, affected systems, risk rating and planned date. Every pull request and deployment references this record.
  2. Impact assessment. The implementer records on the record the security impact, affected customers, dependencies, affected configuration baselines and the rollback plan. If the change introduces a new data type, supplier, hosting region or authentication or encryption design, the Risk Manager completes a targeted risk assessment under the Risk Assessment and Treatment Methodology before approval.
  3. Peer review. Code and configuration changes reach the protected default branch only through a pull request with at least one approving review by someone other than the author. Direct pushes and self-approval are disabled, required checks must pass, and every administrator override, and every change merged without an approving review, is reviewed by the change approver within <Number of business days to review a bypass> business days, with the review recorded on the change record. The quarterly sample in section 5 confirms that every bypass in the quarter was reviewed. Changes that cannot go through a pull request, such as settings in a cloud console, the identity provider, a SaaS admin console, a database or a network device, are described on the change record and approved there before they are made. Approval follows the level in section 1 and comes from someone other than the person making the change. The implementer records on the change record what was changed and when. The quarterly sample in section 5 compares a sample of these records with the admin audit log of each system changed.
  4. Testing. The automated test suite runs on every pull request and must pass before merge. Medium and high-risk changes are also tested in staging, and the result is linked from the change record.
  5. Approval. Approvers record their approval on the change record or pull request before release. CAB decisions are minuted with the change record numbers.
  6. Segregation of duties. No one person writes, approves and releases a change alone. Where a system has too few engineers to separate these duties, the change approver reviews every change released to it within <Number of business days for after-the-fact review> business days and records that review on the change record.
  7. Release. Production releases run only through the deployment pipeline from the protected default branch, with deployment credentials held by the pipeline, not by individuals. Medium and high-risk releases need approval from a named reviewer in the protected production environment. High-risk releases happen within <Standard change window, for example Tuesday to Thursday, 09:00 to 16:00 local time>. The pipeline keeps a history of what was released, from which commit, when and by whom.
  8. Rollback. Medium and high-risk changes carry a written rollback plan before approval, and database migrations carry a tested downgrade or a documented forward fix. If verification fails or <Rollback trigger, for example error rate twice the seven-day baseline for 10 minutes> occurs, the implementer rolls back without further approval and records it.
  9. Verification and review. The implementer confirms the change works in production and records the result. High-risk, failed and rolled-back changes get a post-implementation review within <Number of business days for post-implementation review, for example five> business days, raised as a task in Verity Tasks with an owner and due date. Follow-up actions become further tasks.

3. Environments and configuration baselines

  1. Development, staging and production are separate, with separate cloud accounts or projects and credentials. Standing production access is limited to <Roles with standing production access>.
  2. Production data is not copied to development or staging. Lower environments use masked or synthetic data.
  3. Baseline configurations follow <Configuration baseline standard, for example CIS Benchmarks Level 1> and are kept as code or in version control, with the baseline owner as owner. A change to a baseline is a normal change.
  4. A setting that cannot meet the baseline is recorded as a deviation, with the reason and an expiry date, and approved by <Role that approves baseline deviations, for example the security lead>.
  5. <Tool used to detect configuration drift> reports drift from the baselines. <Role that reviews drift alerts> reviews them <Drift review frequency, for example daily> and records the outcome. Drift that does not match an approved change or deviation is handled under section 5.
  6. The baseline owner reviews each baseline and its deviations at least annually and when the benchmark publishes a new version, and records the review.

4. Emergency changes

  1. An emergency change authorizer approves the change before it is made. The approval and reason are recorded on the change record at the time, or copied there from chat within <Number of hours to record an emergency approval> hours.
  2. A second engineer reviews the change before release where possible, and otherwise as soon as service is restored.
  3. The change approver, or the CAB for a high-risk system, gives retrospective approval by the end of the next business day, tracked as a task in Verity Tasks with that due date. A post-implementation review follows step 9 of section 2.
  4. The number of emergency changes is reported at management review. More than <Emergency change threshold, for example 10 percent of changes in a quarter> triggers a review of why the normal path is not working.

5. Traceability and unauthorized changes

  1. Each quarter the procedure owner samples <Sample size, for example 25 production releases> and traces each from request through approval, peer review and test result to release. The results are attached as evidence to control SD-14.
  2. A release with no approved change record, or drift with no matching change, is handled as a security event under the Incident Response Plan. The root cause and corrective action are tracked as tasks in Verity Tasks.

6. Changes to the ISMS

  1. For a planned change to the ISMS scope, roles, risk method, Statement of Applicability or key suppliers, the ISMS owner records what will change and why, its effect on risks and controls, the people and budget needed, who is responsible and the target date.
  2. <Approver of ISMS changes, for example the executive team> approves the change before it starts. It is tracked as a task in Verity Tasks, affected documents are updated under the Document and Record Control Procedure, and the risk register and Statement of Applicability are updated where affected.

[Optional] For regulated financial institutions: require CAB approval for every change to <Systems the regulator treats as critical, for example core banking and payment systems>, observe change freezes during <Change freeze periods, for example month-end and year-end close>, require two-person authorization for direct production data fixes, require business user acceptance testing with recorded sign-off for changes to those systems, do not use the small-team review in section 2 step 6 for them, keep developers without standing access to their production environments, and notify <Name of the financial regulator> of material changes to critical outsourced services where rules require it.

[Optional] For an on-premises estate: hardware, firmware and network device changes follow this procedure in agreed maintenance windows, with a device configuration backup taken before and after, and any out-of-band console access logged. Changes applied at the primary site are applied at the disaster recovery site within <Number of days to apply changes at the DR site> days and checked, so a failover does not run on an older configuration.

[Optional] For a card data environment: changes to systems in or connected to the card data environment also meet PCI DSS v4.0.1 requirement 6.5 and the significant-change activities in requirements 11.3, 11.4 and 12.5.2. The change record carries a card data impact field, and <Name and job title of the PCI DSS compliance owner> confirms those activities before a significant change is closed.

Records and Evidence

Records are retained for <Retention period for change records, for example three years>. This covers every change, not only the samples, because an auditor picks their own sample from every production release in the period. Where a tool deletes records automatically, for example CI logs that many services delete after 90 days, the procedure owner either sets that tool's retention to the period above or, as part of the quarterly sample in section 5, exports to Verity Evidence the complete list of releases with their pull request, approval and test result.

RecordWhere it is kept
Change records with rating, approval and rollback plan; CAB minutesChange tracking tool; a quarterly sample and the CAB minutes attached as evidence to control SD-01
Pull request reviews, administrator overrides and bypass reviewsSource control and change records; quarterly sample attached as evidence to control SD-06
Automated test resultsCI system; quarterly sample attached as evidence to control SD-02
Deployment historyDeployment pipeline; quarterly sample attached as evidence to control SD-13
Traceability sample results, including the comparison with admin audit logsEvidence attached to control SD-14
Emergency changes and retrospective approvalsChange records and Verity Tasks; each one attached as evidence to control SD-04
Environment separation diagramEvidence attached to control SD-12, refreshed annually
Baselines, approved deviations and baseline reviewsVersion control; the baseline standard, deviation list and annual review attached as evidence to control NS-04
Drift alerts and their outcomeDrift tool; a quarterly summary attached as evidence to control LM-03
Targeted risk assessments triggered by a changeVerity risk register; each one attached as evidence to control GOV-03
Post-implementation reviews and ISMS change recordsTasks in Verity Tasks; ISMS change approvals attached as evidence to control GOV-29

Exceptions

A departure from this procedure is approved in advance by <Role that approves exceptions to this procedure>, recorded as a risk in the Verity risk register with an acceptance and expiry date, and reported at the next management review. No exception removes approval for a high-risk change.

Review

The procedure owner reviews this procedure at least annually, against its review date in Verity Documents, and earlier after a change in source control, CI, deployment or ticketing tools, an incident caused by a change, an audit finding on change management, or the emergency change threshold being exceeded.

Related Documents

  • Secure Development Policy
  • Operations Security Policy
  • Incident Response Plan
  • Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery (BC/DR)
  • Risk Assessment and Treatment Methodology
  • Document and Record Control Procedure
