title: Competence and Awareness Procedure
summary: Defines competence for security roles, how it is evaluated and gaps closed, and the awareness program with phishing exercises and training records.
content_html:
Competence and Awareness Procedure

Company Name: {{company_name}}
Document Owner: <Name and job title of the procedure owner> Version: <Version number, for example 1.0>
Effective Date: <Effective date> Approved By: <Name and job title of the approver>
Last Review: <Date of last review> Next Review: <Date of next review>

1. Purpose

This procedure sets how {{company_name}} defines the competence each security role needs, checks that role holders have it, closes gaps and confirms the actions worked. It also sets the security awareness program, including phishing exercises, and the records that show both operate.

2. Scope

  • Awareness: every employee and contractor working for {{company_name}}.
  • Competence: every person holding a security role listed in section 4, including contractors. Where an outside provider carries out a security role, such as an outsourced internal auditor, security operations service or IT provider, the vendor assessment in Vendors records the competence evidence for the people assigned, checked against section 4 before the work starts.

3. Roles and Responsibilities

Role Responsibilities
Procedure owner Maintains this procedure, the requirements and the competence matrix; runs the awareness program and phishing exercises; reports to management review.
People team Assigns onboarding training, keeps job descriptions current with their security responsibilities and runs performance reviews.
Managers Evaluate competence of staff in security roles, agree gap actions, release time for training and chase overdue training.
Security role holders Keep their competence current, complete assigned actions and provide evidence.
All staff Complete training and policy acknowledgements on time and report suspected phishing.

4. Competence Requirements

The procedure owner keeps these requirements aligned with job descriptions and adds any other role with security duties.

Security role Competence required Acceptable evidence
Security lead Running a security management system, risk assessment and treatment, the frameworks in scope and incident leadership. <Minimum qualification or experience for the security lead, for example CISSP, CISM or five years leading a security program>
System, cloud and database administrators Secure configuration of the platforms in scope, identity and access management, logging, backup and restore, and change control. A platform certification, or a practical assessment by a competent peer.
Software engineers Secure coding in the languages used, common application weaknesses, secrets handling, dependency management and security code review. Secure coding training in the last twelve months and a record of code reviews performed.
On-call incident responders The Incident Response Plan, triage and severity, evidence preservation, escalation and communication. Taking part in a tabletop exercise or a real incident in the last twelve months.
Internal auditors Audit planning, sampling, interviewing, the requirements being audited, writing findings and independence from the work audited. <Minimum training for internal auditors, for example a recognized internal auditor or lead auditor course>, and one audit performed under supervision.
Risk owners and control owners The method in the Risk Management Policy, the risks, controls and evidence they own, and how to raise a deficiency. A briefing by the procedure owner on appointment, recorded in the matrix.

5. Evaluating Competence

  1. Before a person newly appointed to a security role works unsupervised, their manager and the procedure owner compare the person's evidence with section 4. The competence matrix, kept at <Location of the competence matrix, for example a restricted spreadsheet in the HR system>, records, per person and requirement, the evidence seen, any gap, the date and the evaluator.
  2. Competence is evaluated again every twelve months at the performance review, and earlier when new technology comes into scope, an incident or audit finding shows a skills gap, or the role changes.
  3. Self-declaration alone is never accepted as evidence for administrators, incident responders or internal auditors.

6. Closing Gaps

  1. For each gap, the manager and procedure owner choose actions: training, mentoring, supervised practice, reassigning the duty, or hiring or contracting a competent person.
  2. Each action is a task in Tasks with an owner and a due date no more than <Maximum time to close a competence gap, for example 90 days> after the evaluation. The task is given high priority when the gap affects production administration, incident response or internal audit.
  3. Until the gap is closed, the person performs the affected duties only under the supervision of a competent colleague, or the duty is reassigned.
  4. Where nobody in {{company_name}} holds the competence, an external specialist is engaged under the Third-Party Management Policy and recorded in Vendors. Gaps needing budget or headcount go to the next management review.

7. Checking That Actions Worked

  1. Within <Time after an action to check its effect, for example 30 days> of an action finishing, the manager checks that the person can now perform the duty, through a practical assessment, observed work, a test or review of work produced. Attending a course is not proof on its own.
  2. The result is recorded in the matrix and on the task, which is closed only once the check is recorded. If the check fails, a new action is set under section 6.

8. Awareness Program

8.1 Content

The program covers at least:

  • the Information Security Policy and the security objectives that apply to the person's work, where all policies are kept, and the main rules of the Acceptable Use Policy and the Remote Working Policy;
  • data classification and handling, privacy and personal data;
  • phishing, social engineering and payment fraud;
  • passwords, the password manager and multi-factor authentication;
  • device security, working away from the office and safe use of AI tools;
  • how to report a security event, and that good-faith reports are never penalized;
  • the security duties of the person's own role and how doing them well protects customers and {{company_name}}; and what happens when policy is not followed, both the harm a security failure can cause and the disciplinary process.

Role modules add secure coding for engineers, privileged access duties for administrators, access approval and offboarding duties for managers, and payment fraud for finance staff.

8.2 Frequency

  1. New starters complete onboarding security training within <Days after the start date to complete onboarding security training, for example 14> days, and before receiving access to production systems or Confidential customer data.
  2. Everyone completes refresher training every twelve months. Role modules are completed on appointment and every twelve months.
  3. The procedure owner sends a security bulletin on current threats <Frequency of security bulletins, for example monthly>, and within one business day of an active threat targeting staff.
  4. Policies are acknowledged through acknowledgement campaigns in Verity Documents at hire, every twelve months and after a rule changes. A person without a Verity account acknowledges through the alternative method set out in the Acceptable Use Policy.

8.3 Delivery and completion

  1. Training is delivered through <Training platform used for awareness training>. Each module ends with a test with a pass mark of <Pass mark for training tests, for example 80 percent>, and a person who fails retakes it.
  2. Overdue training triggers a reminder on the due date and a notice to the manager seven days later. Training more than 30 days overdue leads to <Action taken when training is more than 30 days overdue, for example suspension of access until completed>.

9. Phishing Exercises

  1. The procedure owner runs simulated phishing exercises for all staff <Frequency of phishing exercises, for example quarterly>, with varied scenarios and targeted ones for finance staff, administrators and executives.
  2. Each exercise is planned in writing and the People team is told before it starts. Scenarios built on distressing personal topics, such as layoffs or health, are not used.
  3. Each exercise measures the share of recipients who clicked, who entered credentials and who reported it, and the time to the first report.
  4. A person who enters credentials receives short training at once. A person who fails <Number of failed exercises in twelve months that triggers coaching, for example three> exercises in twelve months receives one-to-one coaching from the security team.
  5. Results are compared with <Targets for phishing exercises, for example a report rate above 60 percent and credential entry below 5 percent> and used to target training, not to punish. Individual results go only to the person, their manager and the security team.

10. Measuring and Reporting

  1. Every quarter, the procedure owner reports to management review on training completion, test pass rates, phishing results against targets, open competence actions and incidents where human error contributed. Each action decided there becomes a task in Tasks with an owner and due date.
  2. Where a target is missed for two quarters in a row, the procedure owner changes the program content or delivery and records the change in the next report.

[Optional] For regulated financial institutions: board members and senior managers receive a security briefing at least every twelve months, recorded in the board minutes. Staff in roles covered by <Applicable fitness and propriety or certification regime> have their security competence evaluated as part of that regime, and the result is copied to the competence matrix. Hardware security module key custodians and operators of payment systems such as SWIFT are added to section 4. Before they act alone they need evidence of training on the key ceremony or the operator procedures and one supervised run.

[Optional] For a card data environment: the onboarding and yearly training for all staff covers each person's part in protecting card data, phishing and other social engineering that could affect the card data environment, and the acceptable use of end-user technologies. Every person acknowledges the security policies at hire and every twelve months. Completion and acknowledgement are recorded per person (see PCI DSS Requirements 12.6.3, 12.6.3.1 and 12.6.3.2).

[Optional] For on-premises estates: staff working in data centers or server rooms are trained on physical access, visitor escort and equipment handling before being given access.

11. Records and Evidence

Record Where it is kept
Competence requirements per role Attached yearly as evidence to control HR-09; job descriptions attached to control HR-04
Competence matrix Kept live at the location named in rule 5.1; exported after each yearly evaluation and attached as evidence to control HR-09
Competence evidence for people supplied by outside providers The vendor assessment for that provider in Vendors
Actions to close gaps and the checks that they worked Tasks in Tasks, with owner, due date and closure evidence
Training content and yearly schedule Attached yearly as evidence to control HR-08
Training completion and test results Exported quarterly from the training platform and attached as evidence to control HR-08
Onboarding training completion Onboarding checklists attached as evidence to control HR-06
Phishing exercise reports Attached after each exercise as evidence to control HR-08
Policy acknowledgements Acknowledgement campaigns in Verity Documents; the yearly export is attached as evidence to control CS-04
Performance reviews covering security duties The HR system; a yearly completion summary is attached as evidence to control HR-07

These records are kept for <Retention period for training and competence records, for example the length of employment plus three years>.

12. Exceptions

  1. A person showing equivalent current competence, such as a recent certificate, may be excused from a role module. The procedure owner records the equivalence in the matrix.
  2. Nobody is excused from yearly awareness training or phishing exercises. A person on extended leave completes overdue training within 14 days of returning.
  3. Any other exception is approved by <Role that approves exceptions to this procedure> and recorded as a task in Tasks with an owner and an expiry date.

13. Review

The procedure owner reviews this procedure at least every twelve months, using the review date on this document in Verity Documents. An earlier review follows a new security role, an audit finding about competence or awareness, a target missed two quarters in a row, a serious incident caused partly by human error, a new regulatory requirement or a change of training platform.

14. Related Documents

  • Human Resource Security Policy
  • Information Security Roles and Responsibilities Policy
  • Information Security Policy
  • Acceptable Use Policy
  • Remote Working Policy
  • Risk Management Policy
  • Secure Development Policy
  • Incident Response Plan
  • Third-Party Management Policy

15. Revision History

Version Date Author Description of change
<Version number, for example 1.0> <Effective date> <Name and job title of the procedure owner> First approved version.

title: Security Communication Plan
summary: Who communicates which security matters to staff, leadership, customers, suppliers and authorities, when, through which channel and with what approval.
content_html:
Security Communication Plan

Document Type: Standard

Company Name: {{company_name}}
Document Owner: <Name and job title of the document owner> Version: <Version number>
Effective Date: <Date> Approved By: <Name and job title of the approver>
Last Review: <Date> Next Review: <Date>

Purpose

This standard sets which security matters {{company_name}} communicates, to whom, when, how, who sends and approves each message and what record it leaves. It also keeps authority and community contacts current and gives staff one route to report suspected security events. It supports ISO/IEC 27001 clause 7.4 and Annex A controls A.5.5, A.5.6 and A.6.8.

Scope

  • Routine and incident security communication for the {{company_name}} information security management system (ISMS) scope, including marketing claims about security, availability or privacy.
  • Incident handling follows the Incident Response Plan. This standard governs the messages sent during it.

Roles and Responsibilities

  • Plan Owner (<Name and job title of the security officer or ISMS owner>): maintains this standard, its tables and the contact register, runs the quarterly check and reports gaps to management review.
  • Incident Lead: the role named in the Incident Response Plan. Decides when an incident message is needed and obtains its approval.
  • Legal Counsel (<Name of internal counsel or external law firm>): approves every notice to regulators, data subjects, police or the public, and every decision not to notify.
  • Executive Approver (<Job title of the executive who approves incident statements>): approves customer incident notices and public statements with Legal Counsel.
  • All staff and contractors: report suspected events (section 5) and refer outside security questions to the Plan Owner.

Communication Rules

1. General rules

  1. Only the sender named in the matrix sends a security message outside {{company_name}}. Incident, vulnerability and breach messages are approved before sending, and the sender records the approver and time on the incident task.
  2. Messages state what is confirmed, what is still unknown and when the next update follows. They carry no speculation, credentials or unneeded personal data, over channels permitted by the Data Management Policy.
  3. If company email or chat may be compromised or down, the incident team moves to <Backup channel, for example a phone bridge>, using an offline call list. The Plan Owner refreshes the list <Frequency, for example quarterly> and whenever the incident team changes, through a recurring task in Tasks.
  4. Customer, regulator and data subject notice templates, a holding statement and a staff advisory are kept in Verity Documents, approved by Legal Counsel through approval tiers.

2. Communication matrix

Topic Audience Trigger or timing Channel Sender Approver Record kept
Security policies and changes Staff and contractors At hire and on each version that changes what staff must do Acknowledgement campaign in Documents Document owner Document approval tier Campaign results in Documents
Awareness, threat advisories and how to report security events Staff and contractors Onboarding, annual training, <Frequency, for example monthly>, and within one business day of a threat aimed at staff Training and <Internal announcement channel> Plan Owner Plan Owner Training completion records as evidence to control HR-08; quarterly sample as evidence to control CS-06
Confidential route for raising misconduct or security concerns that cannot go through a manager Staff and contractors Onboarding and annual training Training and <Internal announcement channel> <Job title of the owner of the confidential reporting route> Not required Training completion records; anonymized report log as evidence to control CS-05
ISMS performance, audit results, risks above appetite, major incidents Leadership Each management review, and within two business days of a risk above appetite or a major incident Meeting and report Plan Owner Not required Minutes, evidence to control GOV-15
Incident status Incident team and leadership At declaration, then at the interval for the severity in the Incident Response Plan <Incident chat channel> Incident Lead Not required Incident task in Tasks
Incident or personal data breach affecting customers Affected customers Within the customer deadline in section 3 Email to the customer's security contact, then <Status page or account manager call> <Job title of the sender> Legal Counsel and Executive Approver Copy, recipients and send time on the incident task; evidence to control CS-01
Changes to published security commitments or subprocessors Customers <Contractual notice period, for example 30 days> before the change <Trust page or customer email> <Job title of the sender> Plan Owner and Legal Counsel Evidence to control CS-02, or BC-06 for subprocessors
Security terms or incidents involving a supplier Suppliers with access to data or systems At contracting, on terms changes, and when an incident involves the supplier Supplier security contact in Vendors Vendor owner in Vendors Plan Owner, for incident messages Incident task, or evidence to control BC-08
Regulatory notification Authorities in sections 3 and 4 Within the deadline in section 3 The authority's form or portal Authorized contact Legal Counsel and Executive Approver Submission and reference on the incident task; evidence to control DM-01
Suspected crime, for example extortion or fraud Law enforcement When the Incident Lead and Legal Counsel agree to report Route in section 4 Authorized contact Legal Counsel Report reference on the incident task
Public or media statement Public and media Only when an incident is or will become public <Website or press channel> <Job title of the spokesperson> Executive Approver and Legal Counsel Statement on the incident task
Security issues reported by customers, researchers or other outside parties Customers, researchers and the public Acknowledged within <Number of business days>; suspected incidents triaged under section 5 <Published security contact, for example security.txt, a mailbox and the trust page> Plan Owner Plan Owner Task in Tasks for a suspected incident, or finding in Vulnerabilities for a weakness; evidence to control CS-03

3. Notification timelines

The Plan Owner completes this table with Legal Counsel. Each obligation runs on its own clock. Where several customer contracts apply, the incident team works to the shortest contractual deadline. For personal data {{company_name}} processes on a customer's behalf, {{company_name}} notifies the customer, who decides on notice to the authority and to individuals. The authority and individual rows apply to personal data {{company_name}} controls, unless a contract or law says otherwise. The Incident Lead records each clock start on the incident task.

Obligation Recipient Deadline Clock starts
Personal data breach <Name of the data protection authority> <Deadline, for example 72 hours> <Start event, for example becoming aware of the breach>
Breach likely to harm individuals Affected individuals <Deadline> <Start event>
Incident affecting customer data or service Customers <Shortest deadline in customer contracts, in hours> <Start event, for example confirmation of the incident>
National or sector incident reporting <Name of the cyber agency or sector authority, or Not applicable> <Deadline> <Start event>
  1. A decision not to notify is recorded with the reason, Legal Counsel's approval and the time, and attached as evidence to control DM-01.
  2. The Plan Owner rechecks the table at each review, on entering a new country or sector, and when a customer contract with a shorter deadline is signed.

4. Authorities and security communities

Authority or group When to contact Contact route Authorized contact
<Name of the data protection authority> Notifiable personal data breach <Portal, email or phone> <Name and job title>
<Name of the police cybercrime unit> Suspected crime <Reporting route> <Name and job title>
<Name of the national computer emergency response team> Reportable incident or major attack <Reporting route> <Name and job title>
<Names of security communities and alert services> Threat information received and shared Membership or subscription <Name of the person who follows them>
  1. Only the authorized contact speaks to an authority about an incident, after the Incident Lead and Legal Counsel agree. Anyone may call emergency services when life is at risk.
  2. Each authority contact is recorded with date, person, purpose and reference, on the incident task or otherwise as evidence to control CS-07.
  3. The named person reviews community and alert sources at least <Frequency, for example weekly> and logs relevant items and actions as evidence to control LM-12. Sharing outward follows the group's rules, needs Plan Owner approval and never includes customer or personal data.
  4. Once a year, through a recurring task in Tasks, the Plan Owner confirms each contact route works and each membership is active, and attaches the checked register as evidence to control CS-07.

5. Reporting suspected security events

  1. Staff and contractors report a suspected event, weakness or policy breach, such as phishing, a lost device or misdirected data, at once to <Security reporting channel, for example a security mailbox>, or out of hours to <Out-of-hours contact, for example the on-call number>.
  2. Staff report suspicion, not certainty, and do not investigate on their own. A report made in good faith never leads to blame.
  3. The channel is monitored during <Monitoring hours>. The Plan Owner or on-call responder acknowledges each report within <Response time, for example four business hours>, logs it as a task in Tasks with a severity and triages it under the Incident Response Plan.

6. Checking that communication works

  1. Each quarter, through a recurring task in Tasks, the Plan Owner checks a sample of <Number of messages> security messages against the matrix and attaches the result as evidence to control CS-06.
  2. Acknowledgement campaigns below <Completion threshold, for example 95 percent> at their due date are chased within five business days and escalated to managers.
  3. Each incident exercise includes a notification decision and a move to the backup channel. Gaps become tasks in Tasks with an owner and due date.
  4. At each review the Plan Owner compares the matrix with the interested parties register and the compliance obligations register, and adds a row for any party or obligation that needs security communication.

[Optional] For regulated financial institutions: add <Name of the financial regulator>, <Name of the payment system operator> and, for Swift users, Swift's security notification route to sections 3 and 4, each with its incident classification criteria, deadlines and report stages, for example initial, intermediate and final reports. Route every regulator message through <Name of the compliance function>, name a regulator liaison and a deputy, report major incidents to <Name of the board committee> within <Number of hours>, keep a register of regulator submissions with their reference numbers, and join a financial sector information sharing group.

[Optional] For an on-premises estate: add facilities, the data center or colocation operator, utilities and building security to the matrix, and keep a printed call tree in case a site outage takes down email, chat and phones together.

[Optional] For a card data environment: add <Name of the acquiring bank> and each payment brand to sections 3 and 4 with its deadline, report format and route. This supports the notification part of PCI DSS v4.0.1 requirement 12.10.1. The rest of that requirement is met in the Incident Response Plan.

Records and Evidence

Record Where it is kept in Verity Retention
This standard and message templates, with versions and approvals Documents; approved version attached as evidence to control CS-06 While in force, then <Retention period, for example three years>
Staff policy acknowledgments Acknowledgement campaigns in Documents (control CS-04) <Retention period, for example employment plus three years>
Training completion records Evidence attached to control HR-08 <Retention period, for example employment plus three years>
Quarterly message sample; authority and community register and annual check Evidence attached to controls CS-06 and CS-07 <Retention period for ISMS records, for example three years>
Staff event reports, incident notifications, approvals and decisions not to notify Tasks; evidence attached to controls CS-01, CS-03 and DM-01 <Retention period for incident records, for example seven years>
Changes to these records Audit log As set for the audit log

Exceptions

If no approver can be reached and a deadline is at risk, the Incident Lead may send an unaltered approved template, then obtain approval within one business day. Any other departure is approved in advance by <Role that approves exceptions> and recorded as a risk with an acceptance and expiry date.

Review

The Plan Owner reviews this standard at least annually, against its review date in Verity Documents, and earlier after an externally notified incident, an exercise that finds a gap, a new regulator, country or sector, a shorter contractual deadline, or a change of authorized contacts.

Related Documents

  • Incident Response Plan
  • Information Security Policy
  • Information Security Roles and Responsibilities Policy
  • Data Management Policy
  • Third-Party Management Policy
  • Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery (BC/DR)
  • Cloud Services Security Policy

Revision History

Version Date Author Description of change
<Version number> <Date> <Name of the author> First issue, adapted from the Verity template

title: Cloud Services Security Policy
summary: Rules for choosing, configuring, monitoring and exiting cloud services: due diligence, shared responsibility, data location, keys and assurance reviews.
content_html:
Cloud Services Security Policy

Document Type: Policy

Company Name: {{company_name}}
Document Owner: <Name and job title of the document owner> Version: <Version number>
Effective Date: <Date> Approved By: <Name and job title of the approver>
Last Review: <Date> Next Review: <Date>

Purpose

This policy sets how {{company_name}} chooses, sets up, oversees and leaves cloud services. It supports ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A controls A.5.19 to A.5.23 and A.5.30, and SOC 2 criterion CC9.2.

Scope

  • Every cloud infrastructure, platform or software service that holds or processes {{company_name}} or customer information or supports an in-scope service, including free tiers, trials, plugins and services paid by card, and everyone who uses them.

Roles and Responsibilities

  • Security Officer (<Name and job title of the security officer>): owns this policy, tiers services, performs or approves due diligence and reports cloud risks to management review.
  • Platform Lead (<Name and job title of the cloud infrastructure lead>): runs infrastructure and platform services to baseline and owns their keys, logging and resilience design.
  • Service owner: the business owner on the vendor record in Verity Vendors; requests the service and owns its record, renewal and exit.
  • Legal (<Name of the legal or procurement contact>): contract terms, data processing agreements and transfer mechanisms.
  • Executive Approver (<Job title of the executive who approves critical services>): approves critical services and accepts residual risk above appetite.
  • All staff and contractors: use only approved services and never place company or customer data in any other.

Policy

1. Approved services

  1. Approved cloud services are the vendors in Verity Vendors with a recorded, current approval decision. No other service holds company data or connects to company single sign-on.
  2. Before any data is loaded, the requester submits a vendor request in Vendors giving the purpose and the data to be shared. Before approval, the service owner records the data classification, data location and connected systems on the vendor record.
  3. The service owner answers the tiering questionnaire in Vendors, which sets the tier. The Security Officer confirms it and, where it falls below these minimums, overrides it with a recorded justification: critical if it runs production, holds customer confidential or personal data, or its outage stops a customer service; high if it holds other confidential data or has privileged access to company systems; medium for internal data only; low for public data and no connections.
  4. Each production cloud account, subscription or project is recorded in Verity Assets with an owner.
  5. Every <Frequency, for example quarterly>, the Security Officer checks identity provider app grants and card spend for unapproved services, has each one requested or removed within <Number of days> days, and attaches the review as evidence to control BC-05.

2. Due diligence before approval

Tier Minimum due diligence Approved by Reassessed (set in Vendors)
Critical Independent assurance (SOC 2 Type 2 report, ISO/IEC 27001 certificate and scope, or equivalent), questionnaire, data location, subprocessors, section 3 terms, resilience and exit plan Security Officer and Executive Approver <Interval, for example every 12 months>
High Assurance report or questionnaire, data location, subprocessors, breach notice terms, exit plan Security Officer <Interval, for example every 12 months>
Medium Published security information, single sign-on and multi-factor support, data processing agreement for personal data Security Officer <Interval, for example every 24 months>
Low Terms reviewed; no confidential data confirmed Service owner <Interval, for example every 36 months>

For critical and high services, the reviewer records in Vendors:

  1. Report coverage of the service and regions used, for a period ending within <Maximum report age, for example 12 months>, with a bridge letter for any gap.
  2. For a report, the opinion, each exception and its effect on {{company_name}}. For a certificate, that the certification body is accredited, the certificate is in date, and its scope and Statement of Applicability cover the service and locations used, with the certificate recorded in Vendors with its expiry date.
  3. Each complementary user entity control, with the {{company_name}} control and owner that meets it.
  4. Subservice organizations, subprocessors and their locations; key options; logs available to {{company_name}}; handling of government data requests.
  5. The decision, reviewer and date, with residual risk above appetite entered in the risk register for treatment or for acceptance with an expiry date.

3. Contract terms

Contracts for critical and high services include these terms, recorded on the vendor's contract in Vendors. Refused terms are accepted as risks with compensating controls.

  • security and confidentiality duties, and a data processing agreement where personal data is processed;
  • notice of an incident affecting {{company_name}} data within <Maximum hours for provider breach notice> hours;
  • advance notice of new subprocessors and data location changes;
  • an annual assurance report or a right to audit;
  • availability and support service levels;
  • equivalent security and confidentiality duties passed to the provider's own subprocessors, with the provider staying answerable for them;
  • cooperation with {{company_name}} incident investigations, including timely access to relevant logs and records;
  • data returned in a usable format, then deleted with written confirmation within <Number of days> days of termination.

4. Shared responsibility

Responsibility Infrastructure Platform Software
Data centers, hosts and provider network Provider Provider Provider
Operating system, runtime and patching {{company_name}} Provider Provider
Application code, network rules and exposure {{company_name}} Shared Provider
Settings, identities, access, data classification and retention {{company_name}} {{company_name}} {{company_name}}
Encryption, keys, logging, backups, incident detection Shared Shared Shared

This is the default. For each critical and high service, the service owner records the actual split from the provider's published model, names an owner for every item not held by the provider, and attaches it as evidence to control PE-01 for infrastructure and platform providers or BC-08 for others, rechecking it at each reassessment.

5. Configuration baselines

  1. Infrastructure and platform services follow <Baseline standard, for example the CIS Benchmark for each provider>, are built as code where supported, and change only under the Operations Security Policy.
  2. Critical and high software services have a written settings baseline covering at least single sign-on, multi-factor authentication, administrators, external sharing and audit logging.
  3. Root and global administrator accounts use phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication, stay out of daily use and alert the Security Officer on every sign-in.
  4. Production and non-production use separate accounts, subscriptions or projects. Storage is private by default; public resources need recorded approval.
  5. Drift is checked <Frequency, for example weekly> with <Configuration monitoring tool>. Drift that is not an approved deviation is reverted within <Number of days> days or raised as a task in Tasks with an owner and due date. Approved deviations carry a reason, owner and expiry, and the list is attached quarterly as evidence to control NS-04.

6. Data location

  1. Customer and personal data, including backups and replicas, stay in <Approved regions or countries> and any location a customer contract requires. Provider policies block other regions where supported.
  2. A new storage or access location needs Legal approval and, for personal data, a recorded transfer mechanism before the change.

[Optional] For regulated financial institutions: before placing a material function or customer data with a cloud provider, notify or obtain approval from <Name of the financial regulator> as its outsourcing rules require, record it in the outsourcing register, secure audit and access rights for {{company_name}} and the regulator, assess concentration risk, have <Name of the board committee> approve it and its exit strategy, keep customer data in <Countries the regulator permits>, and record the arrangement in the register of outsourcing and third-party technology arrangements the regulator requires.

7. Encryption and keys

  1. Data is encrypted at rest and in transit under the Cryptography Policy.
  2. The key model of each critical and high service (provider-managed, customer-managed or externally held) is recorded at review. Critical services holding customer confidential data use <Required key model, for example customer-managed keys>.
  3. Customer-managed keys separate administration from use, rotate <Rotation interval, for example annually>, have a deletion waiting period and log every use. Records are attached yearly as evidence to control NS-06.

[Optional] For regulated financial institutions: keys that protect customer or payment data in a critical cloud service are generated and held in <Name of the hardware security module or external key manager> under {{company_name}} control, created and destroyed in recorded key ceremonies under dual control and split knowledge, so the provider cannot read the data without {{company_name}}. Ceremony records are attached as evidence to control NS-06.

8. Access and monitoring

  1. Access uses <Identity provider> single sign-on and multi-factor authentication where supported, under the Access Control Policy.
  2. For critical and high services, administrative logs go to <Logging or monitoring tool>, kept <Log retention period>, with alerts at least on root sign-in, identity or logging changes, public resources, key deletion and unapproved regions.
  3. Provider status and security notices go to <Security notice channel>; the Security Officer assesses relevant ones within <Number of business days> business days and raises actions as tasks in Tasks. A provider notice of an incident that affects or may affect {{company_name}} data or service is reported at once under the Incident Response Plan, and the time of the notice is recorded on the incident task as the possible start of the deadlines in the Security Communication Plan.

9. Ongoing oversight and resilience

  1. Each service is reassessed by its next reassessment date in Vendors, or sooner after a new data type or region, a provider incident, a qualified opinion or a change of provider ownership.
  2. For each provider hosting production, the Security Officer reviews the current assurance report at least annually, confirms {{company_name}} operates each complementary user entity control, and attaches the review as evidence to control PE-01. Any {{company_name}} SOC 2 report names the provider as a subservice organization.
  3. Service owners record measured service levels of critical services in Vendors <Frequency, for example quarterly> and raise shortfalls.
  4. Critical services have recovery objectives in the Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery (BC/DR) plan. Production workloads on infrastructure or platform services span at least <Minimum number of availability zones> availability zones, with backups in a separate account and region. Annual BC/DR testing includes a provider or region outage.

10. Exit

  1. Before a critical or high service is approved, the service owner records an exit plan covering export method and format, export time, replacement and dependencies, and attaches it as evidence to control BC-08. For critical services a test export runs <Frequency, for example every two years>, with the result attached as evidence to control BC-08.
  2. On exit, within <Number of days> days of contract end, the service owner exports and verifies the data, removes integrations, API keys, service accounts and single sign-on, revokes customer-managed keys, obtains written deletion confirmation, and records access revocation and data return in the vendor's offboarding in Vendors.

[Optional] For an on-premises estate: record hybrid links such as VPNs and directory synchronization in Assets and in the responsibility split, and apply section 6 to replicated data.

[Optional] For a card data environment: tag in Vendors each provider that stores, processes or transmits card data or can affect the security of the card data environment, with the services it provides. Before engaging it, include in its contract that it is accountable for protecting the card data it holds or handles for {{company_name}} and for its effect on the card data environment. Obtain its PCI DSS attestation of compliance for the services used before engagement and at least every 12 months, and record from its responsibility matrix which requirements the provider meets, which {{company_name}} meets and which are shared. This supports PCI DSS v4.0.1 requirements 12.8.1 to 12.8.5.

Records and Evidence

Record Where it is kept in Verity Retention
Approved services: tier, owners, data location, contracts, decision, reassessment date, offboarding Vendors (controls BC-07 and BC-08); data processing agreements also as evidence to control DM-10 Life of the service plus <Retention period, for example six years>
Assurance reports and their reviews, responsibility splits, exit plans and exit tests Vendor documents and report reviews in Vendors; evidence attached to controls PE-01 and BC-08 Life of the service plus <Retention period>
Baseline deviations, key records, unapproved service reviews Evidence attached to controls NS-04, NS-06 and BC-05 <Retention period for ISMS records, for example three years>
Accepted cloud risks and contract gaps; production cloud accounts Risk register, with acceptance and expiry; Assets <Retention period for ISMS records>

Exceptions

A departure is approved in advance by the Security Officer, or the Executive Approver for a critical service, and recorded in the risk register with an acceptance expiring within <Maximum exception period, for example 12 months>.

Review

The Security Officer reviews this policy at least annually, against its review date in Verity Documents, and earlier after a new infrastructure provider, a provider breach or major outage, a new data location requirement, a cloud audit finding or an ISMS scope change.

Related Documents

  • Third-Party Management Policy
  • Cryptography Policy
  • Access Control Policy
  • Operations Security Policy
  • Data Management Policy
  • Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery (BC/DR)
  • Risk Management Policy
  • Security Communication Plan

title: Operating Procedure Template
summary: A template copied once per operating procedure: owner, access, numbered steps, schedule, escalation, restart and records in Verity, with a starter list of procedures to write.
content_html:
Operating Procedure Template

Document Type: Procedure

Company Name:{{company_name}}
Procedure Owner:<Name and job title of the procedure owner>Version: <Version number>
Effective Date:<Date>Approved By: <Name and job title of the approver>
Last Review:<Date>Next Review: <Date>

Purpose

This procedure sets out how {{company_name}} performs <Name of the operating activity, for example restoring a production database from backup> on <System or service the procedure covers>, so the work is done the same way every time, only by authorized people, and leaves a record. Procedures written from this template support SOC 2 criterion CC5.3 through Verity control GOV-17 and, in a workspace that has added ISO 27001, ISO/IEC 27001 control A.5.37 through Verity control GOV-28, which also keeps them as controlled documents. Procedures for backups, logging, monitoring or changes also support A.8.13, A.8.15, A.8.16 or A.8.32 by reference, carrying out the rule the related policy sets.

Scope

  • Systems and environments: <Systems, environments and accounts this procedure covers>.
  • Sites: <Sites or regions where the procedure is performed, or cloud only>.
  • People: <Role or group that performs the procedure>, including contractors working for {{company_name}}.
  • Out of scope: <Related activities this procedure does not cover and the procedure that does>.

Roles and Responsibilities

  • Procedure owner (<Name and job title of the procedure owner>): keeps the steps accurate, takes each new version through approval, runs the acknowledgement campaign and reviews the procedure by its review date.
  • Operators (<Role or group that performs the procedure>): follow only the published version, record each run and tell the owner when a step no longer matches the system.
  • Approver (<Name and job title of the approver>): approves or rejects each new version in its approval tier.
  • Escalation contacts: the people listed in Procedure step 4, Error handling and escalation, who decide next steps when a run fails.
  • ISMS owner: keeps the list of required operating procedures in the Verity Documents register and confirms each in-scope system has the procedures it needs.

Using This Template

  1. Create one document per operating procedure in Verity Documents from this template, titled <System or activity> Operating Procedure, owned by the procedure owner and linked to control GOV-17, to GOV-28 where ISO 27001 is added, and to the Verity controls the starter list names for it.
  2. Replace every prompt in angle brackets and keep every procedure heading. Where a section does not apply, write "Not applicable" and why.
  3. Approve the procedure through the approval tiers in the Document and Record Control Procedure, then run an acknowledgement campaign for the operators' role or group on first publication and after every material change.
  4. Remove this section and the starter list from each copy before approval. The starter list stays in this template for the next copy, and the required procedures are tracked in the Verity Documents register, as the Document and Record Control Procedure sets out.

Starter List of Operating Procedures

Write at least these procedures for every in-scope system they apply to, and add any others that your risk assessment or customers require. Incident runbooks sit under the Incident Response Plan.

ProcedureWhat it coversVerity controls and ISO 27001 references
System build and configurationBuilding servers, images, cloud accounts and network devices to the approved baseline, and checking for driftNS-04, LM-03, A.8.9
Backup and restoreBackup schedule, failure handling, restore requests and the periodic restore testBC-01, BC-02, A.8.13
Monitoring and alert handlingAlerts, including capacity and performance thresholds, who receives them, triage, escalation and tuningLM-09, BC-04, A.8.16, A.8.6
Job schedulingScheduled and automated jobs, their dependencies, start and finish checks, and rerunsSD-08
Log managementLog sources, retention, protection, review and checks for sources that stop sendingLM-02, A.8.15
Access administrationGranting, changing and removing access, privileged access and access reviewsIAM-01, IAM-02, IAM-07, IAM-12, A.5.18, A.8.2
Production deploymentReleasing approved changes to production, checks after release and rollbackSD-13, A.8.32
Key and secret rotationRotating keys, certificates and secrets on schedule and after a suspected exposure, and hardware security module key ceremoniesNS-06, A.8.24
Media handling (where tapes, disks or removable media are used)Labeling, storing, moving and destroying tapes, disks and removable mediaDM-16, A.7.10, A.7.14
End of day batch processing (core banking and other batch systems)Batch order, cutoff times, reconciliation of totals and rules for rerunsSD-08
Data center operations (own data centers and DR sites only)Entry and visitor escort, power, cooling and fire checks, equipment maintenance and DR site readinessA.7.2, A.7.11, A.7.13, A.5.30

Procedure

1. Prerequisites and access needed

  • Access: <Accounts, roles or permissions needed, for example the backup operator role>. Access comes through access provisioning, is held by named people and is never shared.
  • Privileged access: <How elevated access is obtained, for example just in time elevation through the bastion host>.
  • Credentials: <Secrets vault or password manager holding this procedure's credentials>. Passwords, keys and tokens are never written here.
  • Tools: <Tools, scripts or consoles used, with their location>.
  • Before starting: <Approvals or conditions needed first, for example an approved change or an open maintenance window>.

2. Schedule or trigger

  • Schedule: <When the procedure runs, for example daily at 01:00 UTC, or Not applicable>. Each scheduled run or periodic check is a recurring task in Verity Tasks owned by <Role or group that performs the procedure>, with the SLA level <SLA level whose resolve time fits each run, for example one business day> setting its deadline.
  • Trigger: <Event or request that starts the procedure, for example a restore request or an alert>. A triggered run gets a task with an owner in Verity Tasks before work starts.
  • Dependencies: <Jobs or procedures that must finish before this one starts, and those that wait for it>.

3. Steps

  1. <Step 1: action, command or screen, and expected result>
  2. <Step 2: action, command or screen, and expected result>
  3. <Step 3: action, command or screen, and expected result>
  4. Confirm the outcome: <How the operator confirms success, for example record counts match or the restored service passes its health check>.
  5. Record the run as described in Records and Evidence, then close the task.

Write each step so a trained newcomer can follow it unaided. A step that changes production follows the Change Management Procedure. The only exceptions are standard changes already in the standard change catalog in Verity Documents: <Standard changes from the catalog that this procedure covers, or None>. Naming a change here does not make it a standard change.

4. Error handling and escalation

  1. When a step fails or gives an unexpected result, the operator stops, records the error and actions taken on the task, and retries no more than <Number of retries allowed before escalating> times.
  2. Known errors and their fixes: <Common errors, their likely cause and the approved fix>.
  3. Anything else is escalated using the contacts below; a suspected security event goes straight to the Incident Response Plan.
LevelContactHow to reachWhen to escalate
1<Primary on-call role or person><Paging tool, phone or channel><Condition, for example a failed run or retries exhausted>
2<Secondary contact or team lead><Paging tool, phone or channel><Condition, for example no response within 30 minutes>
3<Service or system owner><Paging tool, phone or channel><Condition, for example customer impact or data at risk>
Supplier<Supplier support contact, if any><Support portal or phone and contract reference><Condition, for example a fault in the supplier's service>

5. Restart and recovery

  1. Safe restart point: <Step a failed run restarts from, and what to check first>.
  2. Undoing partial work: <How to roll back or clean up a run that stopped part way>.
  3. Before resuming service, the operator confirms <Integrity checks before resuming, for example totals reconcile and no duplicate records exist>. If data must be restored, follow <Name of the backup and restore procedure>.
  4. The run is complete when <Criteria for declaring the run or recovery complete>. The operator records the cause, recovery steps and outcome on the task.
  5. Keep an offline copy for outages at <Location of the offline copy of critical runbooks>, refreshed with each new version.

[Optional] For regulated financial institutions: name in each procedure the role accountable for it and the role that performs it. Keep whoever runs a batch or job separate from whoever approves its reconciliation, run privileged steps under dual control or in a recorded privileged session, and take changes to core banking systems through the change advisory board. Keep run records for the period set by <Name of the financial regulator>, and confirm through acknowledgement campaigns that every operator knows the current version, so procedures are current and ready for regulatory examination.

[Optional] For a card data environment: keep an operating procedure for the activities of each PCI DSS requirement, 1 to 12, that your teams carry out. Each procedure names the roles that perform it and the people who hold them, is reviewed by its review date and whenever the environment changes, and is followed in practice. Operators confirm through an acknowledgement campaign that they know the current version and understand their role. Assessors compare the steps with actual practice, so record each run in Verity Tasks.

Records and Evidence

RecordWhere it is kept in Verity
Procedure versions, approvals and review datesVerity Documents (control GOV-17, and GOV-28 where ISO 27001 is added)
Operator acknowledgementsThe acknowledgement campaign on this document in Verity Documents
Completed runs, with date, operator, result and any deviationClosed tasks in Verity Tasks
Run output, such as job logs, restore tests or alert reviewsEvidence attached to <Verity control the procedure supports, for example BC-02>
Errors, escalations and recovery notesThe task for that run in Verity Tasks

Records follow the retention periods in the Document and Record Control Procedure.

Exceptions

An operator who departs from a step records the reason on the task and tells the procedure owner the same day. A standing departure needs advance approval from the procedure owner and the ISMS owner, recorded as a risk in the Verity risk register with an acceptance and expiry date. Emergency work follows the emergency change route in the Change Management Procedure.

Review

The procedure owner reviews this procedure at least every 12 months, or more often where <Shorter review interval for this procedure, if any> applies, and earlier when the system changes, after a failed run or incident the procedure contributed to, and after an audit finding. Approved system changes include updating the affected procedure. Each review updates the review date in Verity Documents and goes through Tier 1 approval, even with no other change.

Related Documents

  • Operations Security Policy
  • Document and Record Control Procedure
  • Change Management Procedure
  • Incident Response Plan
  • Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery (BC/DR)
  • Access Control Policy
  • Asset Management Policy

Revision History

VersionDateAuthorDescription of change

title: Information Security Policy Statement
summary: One page statement by top management that commits to meeting security requirements, to improving the program and to setting objectives, signed by the executive sponsor.
content_html:
Issued by: {{legal_name}}, {{registered_address}}. Owned by: {{security_lead}}. Approved by: {{executive_sponsor}}.

Information Security Policy Statement

Document Type: Policy

Company Name:{{company_name}}
Document Owner:<Name and job title of the ISMS owner>Version: <Version number, for example 1.0>
Effective Date:<Effective date>Approved By: <Name and job title of the executive sponsor>
Last Review:<Date of last review>Next Review: <Date of next review>

Statement

{{company_name}} <Short description of what the company does and for whom>. Our customers and partners trust us with their information. Protecting it is part of how we run the business, not a side project.

Top management sets this statement. It applies to everyone who works for or on behalf of {{company_name}}, and to every system, site and supplier inside the scope of our security program.

Our Commitments

  1. We meet our requirements. We find the legal, regulatory and contractual requirements and the promises we make to customers that bear on security, and we meet them. Each one has a named owner in the Context and Interested Parties Register.
  2. We keep improving. We look for weaknesses through risk assessment, monitoring, internal audit, incidents and feedback, and we fix their causes. Top management reviews the program at least once a year and acts on what it finds.
  3. We set objectives and measure them. Each year we set measurable security objectives that follow from our risks and requirements. Each has an owner, a target and a date. They are kept in the Information Security Objectives and Plan and checked at every management review.
  4. We give the program what it needs. Top management assigns the roles, budget, time and tools these commitments need, and holds named owners to account.
  5. We tell people. This statement and the policies under it are published to all staff in Documents. Everyone acknowledges them when they join and every year after. We share this statement with customers, suppliers and others who ask for it.

How This Statement Is Used

  1. The topic policies, standards and procedures in Documents put this statement into practice. Each is approved by its accountable manager and reviewed at least once a year.
  2. Everyone follows them and reports a security concern or incident at once through <Security reporting channel, for example a security email address or chat channel>.
  3. Breaking a security policy on purpose or through serious carelessness is handled through the disciplinary process.

Approval

Signed bySignatureDate
<Name and job title of the executive sponsor><Signature or electronic approval reference><Date signed>

Records and Evidence

RecordWhere it is kept in Verity
Signed statement, every versionDocuments, with the approval record; attached as evidence to control GOV-17
Staff acknowledgementsAcknowledgement campaign in Documents (control CS-04)

Review

Top management reviews this statement at every management review, and after a major change to the business, its risks or its requirements. Each new version is signed again and sent to all staff for acknowledgement.

Related Documents

  • Information Security Policy
  • ISMS Scope Statement
  • Context and Interested Parties Register
  • Information Security Objectives and Plan
  • Management Review Procedure and Minutes

title: ISMS Operating Plan
summary: How the recurring security activities are scheduled, run and checked, how changes to the ISMS and outsourced work are controlled, and the record each one leaves.
content_html:
ISMS Operating Plan

Document Type: Standard

Company Name:{{company_name}}
Document Owner:<Name and job title of the ISMS owner>Version: <Version number, for example 1.0>
Effective Date:<Effective date>Approved By: <Name and job title of the executive sponsor>
Last Review:<Date of last review>Next Review: <Date of next review>

Purpose

This plan sets out how {{company_name}} runs the processes of its information security management system (ISMS) as planned, how it controls changes to them, and how it controls security work that others do on its behalf. Each activity has an owner, a schedule, a standard for done and a record in Verity, so anyone can see what ran, what is late and what was missed. It supports ISO/IEC 27001 clauses 4.4, 6.3 and 8.1 and Verity control GOV-29.

Scope

Every recurring activity that keeps the ISMS and the controls in the Statement of Applicability running, every planned change to the ISMS, and every security process that a supplier, contractor or group company performs for {{company_name}} inside the ISMS scope.

Roles and Responsibilities

  • ISMS owner (<Name and job title of the ISMS owner>): maintains this plan, sets up the recurring tasks, reviews progress each month and reports to management review.
  • Executive sponsor (<Name and job title of the executive sponsor>): approves this plan, the resources it needs and the changes in section 4 that move the scope, the risk method or the budget.
  • Activity owners: run each activity on time, to the standard in section 2, and attach the record it leaves. The roles named in section 2 are mapped to people in the Information Security Roles and Responsibilities Policy.
  • Vendor owners: hold the agreement and the assurance for each outsourced process in section 5 and check it at each supplier review.

1. How Planned Activities Run

  1. Each activity in section 2 is a recurring task in Tasks with an owner, a due date and the record it must leave. A task without an owner is not allowed.
  2. An activity is done only when its record is attached and meets the Done when column. A task closed without its record counts as not done.
  3. Each activity follows its written procedure in Documents. Where none exists, the owner writes one from the Operating Procedure Template before the first run.
  4. An owner may run an activity early. Running it late needs the ISMS owner's approval, recorded on the task with the reason and a new date.
  5. A missed or failed activity is raised as an issue under the Corrective Action and Improvement Procedure.

2. Operating Calendar

The frequencies below are the minimum. Where a control, contract or regulator asks for more, the stricter one applies.

ActivityOwnerFrequencyDone whenRecord in Verity
Risk assessmentISMS ownerYearly and after a significant changeEvery asset group in scope assessed, risks rated, owners namedRisk register; report as evidence on GOV-18
Risk treatment and acceptance reviewRisk owners<Frequency of risk treatment reviews, for example quarterly>Each treatment on track or replanned, each acceptance inside its expiryRisk register; evidence on GOV-20
Statement of Applicability reviewISMS ownerYearly and after each risk assessmentEvery decision has a current reason and the new version is approvedApplicability page in Frameworks; export on GOV-27
User access reviewsSystem ownersQuarterlyEvery account reviewed, changes made and signed offEvidence on IAM-02
Privileged access reviewSecurity leadQuarterlyEvery privileged account and tool justified or removedEvidence on IAM-07
Vulnerability scanning and triageEngineering lead<Scan frequency, for example weekly>Every finding triaged inside its timeframeVulnerabilities; evidence on LM-11
Patch compliance reportIT leadMonthlyDevices outside the patch timeframe followed upEvidence on EP-04
Backup restore testEngineering lead<Restore test frequency, for example quarterly>Restore completed and time measured against the targetEvidence on BC-02
Continuity and recovery exerciseBusiness continuity ownerYearlyExercise run, gaps raised as issuesEvidence on BC-03
Incident tabletop exerciseSecurity leadYearlyExercise report written and actions raisedEvidence on LM-10
Security awareness trainingPeople leadAt joining and yearlyEvery member of staff has completed itEvidence on HR-08
Phishing exerciseSecurity lead<Phishing exercise frequency, for example quarterly>Results reported, repeat clickers retrainedEvidence on HR-08
Policy reviewDocument ownersYearlyEach document reviewed and approved againDocuments; evidence on GOV-01
Supplier reviewsVendor ownersYearly for critical suppliersAssurance in date and issues followed upVendors; evidence on BC-08
Cloud provider assurance reviewVendor owner of the providerYearlyReport read, customer duties confirmedVendors; evidence on PE-01
Asset inventory reconciliationIT leadQuarterlyAssets matched to billing and identity recordsAssets; evidence on LM-01
Log review and alert tuningSecurity leadDaily review through alerts, tuning quarterlyTuning review recordedEvidence on LM-02 and LM-09
Capacity reviewEngineering leadQuarterlyReview and actions recordedEvidence on BC-04
Objectives measurementObjective owners<Measurement frequency, for example quarterly>Results recorded against targetsEvidence on GOV-26
Penetration testSecurity leadYearly and after a major changeReport received, findings tracked to closureEvidence on GOV-16
Internal auditAudit program managerAs the audit program setsReport issued and findings raisedEvidence on GOV-13
Management reviewExecutive sponsor<Management review frequency, for example twice a year>Minutes approved and actions raisedEvidence on GOV-15
Legal and contract requirements reviewISMS ownerYearlyRegister current and owners confirmedContext and Interested Parties Register
Authority and community contacts checkISMS ownerYearlyEach contact confirmed workingEvidence on CS-07

3. Watching the Plan

  1. Each month the ISMS owner reviews Tasks for activities due, done, late and missed, and writes a short status note on the monthly review task.
  2. Each quarter the ISMS owner reports the completion rate and every late or missed activity to the executive sponsor. The report is attached as evidence to control GOV-29.
  3. Management review receives the completion rate for the year, the missed activities and what was done about them.
  4. Once a year the ISMS owner checks this plan against the Statement of Applicability, so that every applicable control with a recurring duty has a row in section 2.

4. Changing the ISMS

  1. A change to the ISMS includes a change to its scope, policies, roles, risk method, control set, tools or key suppliers, and any reorganization that moves security duties.
  2. Before the change, the person proposing it raises a task in Tasks for the ISMS owner that records the reason and the expected result, the risks and side effects, including effects on other controls, the owner, the timing, and the people, budget and tools needed.
  3. The ISMS owner checks that the ISMS still works as a whole after the change: no duty without an owner, no control without a record, and no gap in a scheduled activity while the change happens.
  4. The executive sponsor approves changes that move the scope, the risk method or the resources. The ISMS owner approves the others. The decision is recorded on the task.
  5. Changes to production systems follow the Change Management Procedure, not this section.
  6. After an unplanned change, such as a sudden reorganization or the loss of a supplier, the ISMS owner reviews its effects within <Number of business days to review an unplanned change> business days and raises an issue for any harm found.

5. Outsourced Processes

  1. An outsourced process is security work that someone outside {{company_name}} does for it, such as managed hosting, a managed detection service, background screening or an outside internal auditor.
  2. For each one, the vendor owner records the standard the supplier must meet in the contract or service agreement, how {{company_name}} checks it, and who is accountable inside {{company_name}}. Accountability for the result stays with {{company_name}}.
  3. Each outsourced process is checked at the supplier review in Vendors. Any shortfall is raised as an issue.
Outsourced processSupplierStandard set inHow it is checkedAccountable owner
<Outsourced process, for example managed detection and response><Supplier name><Contract or service agreement reference><How the work is checked, for example a monthly report and a yearly assurance review><Accountable owner inside the company>

Records and Evidence

RecordWhere it is kept in Verity
This plan, every versionDocuments, with approvals; attached as evidence to control GOV-29
Records that planned activities were doneThe record on each recurring task in Tasks and on the control named in section 2; the quarterly completion report on GOV-29
Reviews of planned and unplanned changesThe change task in Tasks, with the decision; attached as evidence to GOV-29
Checks of outsourced processesThe supplier's record in Vendors; a yearly summary attached to GOV-29

Records are kept for <Retention period for ISMS records, for example three years after the record is superseded>.

Exceptions

An activity may be paused only with the executive sponsor's approval, recorded on its task with the reason, the risk and a restart date. Every paused activity is reported at the next management review.

Review

The ISMS owner reviews this plan at least once a year, after each risk assessment, after each change under section 4, and whenever a control is added to or removed from the Statement of Applicability.

Related Documents

  • ISMS Scope Statement
  • Information Security Objectives and Plan
  • Operating Procedure Template
  • Change Management Procedure
  • Third-Party Management Policy
  • Corrective Action and Improvement Procedure
  • Management Review Procedure and Minutes
