title: SOC 2 System Description
summary: Management's description of the system for a SOC 2 examination: services, commitments, the five components, incidents, criteria and controls, customer and subservice controls, criteria that do not apply and changes.
content_html:
Service organisation: {{legal_name}}, {{registered_address}}.

SOC 2 System Description

Document Type: Charter

Company Name:{{company_name}}
Document Owner:<Name and job title of the description owner>Version: <Version number, for example 1.0>
Effective Date:<Effective date>Approved By: <Name and job title of the executive sponsor>
Last Review:<Date of last review>Next Review: <Date of next review>

Purpose

This document is the description of the {{company_name}} system that management gives to the service auditor for a SOC 2 examination. It tells readers of the report what the system does, what {{company_name}} has promised, how the system is built and run, and which controls others must operate. The service auditor examines it against the description criteria (DC 200). It supports SOC 2 criteria CC2.2, CC2.3 and CC3.1 and Verity controls GOV-22 and PE-01.

Scope

One description covers one system for one report. Write a separate description for each system that has its own report.

ItemDetail
System name<Name of the system covered by this description>
Report type<Type 1 at a date, or Type 2 for a period>
Report date or period<Date for a Type 1, or start and end dates for a Type 2>
Categories in scopeSecurity, plus <Other trust services categories in scope, for example availability and confidentiality, or none>
Service auditor<Name of the audit firm>

Roles and Responsibilities

  • Executive sponsor (<Name and job title of the executive sponsor>): approves the description and signs management's assertion.
  • Description owner (<Name and job title of the description owner>): drafts and maintains the description, gathers input, reconciles it with Verity records and works through review comments with the service auditor.
  • Contributors: the engineering lead writes sections 3.1, 3.2 and 3.5, the people lead section 3.3, the ISMS owner sections 3.4, 4, 5 and 9, and the vendor owners section 7.

Using This Template

  1. Write for a reader who knows nothing about {{company_name}}, such as a customer's security team. Describe what actually happens, not what should happen.
  2. Every statement must be true for the whole report date or period. If something changed during the period, say so in section 9.
  3. Keep the description consistent with the ISMS Scope Statement, Assets, Vendors and the controls in Frameworks. Reconcile any difference before the description is issued.
  4. Leave out marketing claims. The auditor can test anything written here.
  5. Call the result a SOC 2 report or a SOC 2 examination, the way the audit firm does, and use no other term for it with customers.
  6. Management's assertion is a separate signed statement that goes with this description. The audit firm supplies its format and wording. It is not part of this template.

1. Company Overview and Services

<Short history of the company, where it operates and how many people it employs>

<Services covered: what each does, who uses it and how customers reach it>

Not covered by this description: <Services, products or locations outside this description, or none>.

2. Service Commitments and System Requirements

  1. Service commitments are promises {{company_name}} makes to customers about the system, in contracts, service level agreements, terms of service, the security page and the privacy notice.
  2. System requirements are what the system must do to keep those promises and to meet the laws, regulations, standards and internal policies that apply.
  3. {{company_name}} designs its controls to meet these commitments and requirements. The table shows the main ones.
Commitment or requirementWhere it is madeCategory
<Commitment, for example customer data is encrypted in transit and at rest><Where it is made, for example the master services agreement and the security page>Security
<Commitment, for example a monthly availability target><Where it is made, for example the service level agreement><Category>
<Law, regulation or standard that applies to the system><What it requires of the system><Category>

How commitments reach customers: <How commitments are shared with customers, for example contracts, onboarding material and the trust page>.

3. The Five System Components

Describe each component as it was during the report period. Anything not listed here is outside the system.

3.1 Infrastructure

ComponentProvider or locationPurposeRegion
<Infrastructure component, for example production cloud account, database service or content delivery network><Provider or location><Purpose><Region>

<Network design: how environments are separated and how traffic reaches the system>

3.2 Software

Application or serviceWhat it doesBuilt or bought
<Application or service name><What it does><Built in house or bought>

Supporting tools: <Supporting software, for example the identity provider, source control, deployment pipeline, monitoring and ticketing tools>.

3.3 People

<Organization structure: the teams that build, run and support the system, with headcount and reporting lines>

<Oversight body and how it oversees security, for example the board or executive team meeting quarterly>

<Name of the security officer role and who it reports to>

3.4 Procedures

<Main procedures that run the system, automated and manual, and the documents in Documents that define them, for example access, change, monitoring, incident response, backup and recovery, vendor management and data handling>

3.5 Data

Data typeClassificationWhere it is storedRetention
<Data type, for example customer content, account data or logs><Classification><Where it is stored><Retention period>

<How data enters, moves through and leaves the system, with a reference to the data flow diagram>

4. Criteria and Related Controls

  1. For each category in scope, the controls that address each criterion are listed in the controls section of the report, prepared with the service auditor. Export the mapped controls from Frameworks as the starting point, and check that each has an owner and evidence in Verity.
  2. Describe in a short paragraph each of the following, because readers look for them:
  • Control environment: <How leadership sets expectations, for example the oversight body, code of conduct, hiring checks, training and performance reviews>
  • Risk assessment: <How risks to the commitments are found and rated, how often, and who approves the treatment>
  • Information and communication: <How policies and security information reach staff, customers and suppliers, including the reporting channels>
  • Monitoring: <How controls are monitored, for example automated checks, internal audit, penetration tests and management review>
  • Control activities: <Summary of the main control activities for access, change, operations, incidents, continuity and vendors>
  1. Mark every control that depends on a customer (section 6) or a subservice organization (section 7).

5. Incidents in the Period

  1. Disclose each incident in the report period that caused {{company_name}} to miss a service commitment or system requirement, or was likely to. For each, state what happened, when, what it affected and what was done.
  2. The ISMS owner builds the list from the incident register in Tasks and the postmortems on control LM-05, and records why each other incident did not qualify.
IncidentDateEffect on commitmentsActions taken
<Incident summary, or none><Date of the incident><Effect on commitments><Actions taken>

6. Controls Expected of Customers

  1. Some criteria are met only when customers do their part. These are often called complementary user entity controls. List each control {{company_name}} expects customers to run, and the criteria it supports.
  2. Check that each one is also stated in the contract or customer documentation.
Control expected of customersRelated criteria
Customers manage their own users, roles and access reviews in the product<Related criteria>
Customers protect the credentials and keys they use to reach the service<Related criteria>
Customers tell {{company_name}} promptly about suspected security incidents on their account<Related criteria>
<Other control expected of customers><Related criteria>

7. Subservice Organizations

  1. A subservice organization is a supplier whose service is part of the system and whose controls are needed to meet the criteria, such as the cloud hosting provider.
  2. Agree one method for each with the service auditor:
  • Carve out: the supplier's controls are left out of the examination. The description names the supplier, the services it provides and the controls {{company_name}} expects it to run, often called complementary subservice organization controls. {{company_name}} monitors those controls, for example by reading the supplier's own SOC 2 report each year.
  • Inclusive: the supplier's relevant controls are described here and tested as part of this examination. This needs the supplier's agreement and its own written assertion.
  1. Each subservice organization is recorded in Vendors. At least once a year its vendor owner reads its assurance report, checks that it covers the services and regions used, notes any exceptions, and confirms that {{company_name}} runs the customer controls that report expects, as control PE-01 requires.
Subservice organizationServices usedMethodControls expected of itRelated criteriaHow it is monitored
<Cloud hosting provider><Hosting services used><Carve out or inclusive>Physical security of data centers, environmental protection, hardware disposal<Related criteria>Yearly review of its assurance report in Vendors
<Other subservice organization><Services used><Carve out or inclusive><Controls expected of it><Related criteria><How it is monitored>

8. Criteria That Do Not Apply

A criterion does not apply only when the situation it covers does not exist in this system. A missing control is never a reason.

CriterionWhy it does not apply
<Criterion identifier, or none><Reason it does not apply to this system>

9. Significant Changes in the Period

For a Type 2 report, describe significant changes during the period, such as a new service, a move of infrastructure, a new subservice organization, a change to a key control or a change of key people. Draw them from change records and the change triggered risk reviews on control GOV-03.

ChangeDateEffect on the system and controls
<Significant change, or none><Date of the change><Effect on the system and controls>

Records and Evidence

RecordWhere it is kept in Verity
Approved description, every versionDocuments, with approvals; attached as evidence to control GOV-22
Commitments and requirementsSection 2, with the contracts and pages it cites, attached to GOV-22
Subservice organization reviewsThe supplier's record in Vendors; attached as evidence to control PE-01
Reconciliation with Assets, Vendors and FrameworksA review task in Tasks for each issued version

Exceptions

None. A known inaccuracy is corrected before the description is issued, or disclosed in it with the service auditor's agreement.

Review

The description owner reviews this description before each examination, at least once a year, and after any significant change to the system. At each review the owner reconciles it with Assets, Vendors, Frameworks, the ISMS Scope Statement and what is deployed, and records each difference and its fix. The executive sponsor approves each issued version through the approval tiers in Documents. The issued description is confidential and is shared outside {{company_name}} only inside the SOC 2 report or under a confidentiality agreement.

Related Documents

  • Context and Interested Parties Register
  • Risk Assessment and Treatment Methodology
  • Third-Party Management Policy

  • Incident Response Plan
  • Change Management Procedure

title: Business Impact Analysis
summary: Rates how harm grows when each service or activity stops, sets recovery time and data loss targets, maps dependencies, checks the technology can meet them and records the insurance decision.
content_html:
Business Impact Analysis

Document Type: Standard

Company Name:{{company_name}}
Document Owner:<Name and job title of the business continuity owner>Version: <Version number, for example 1.0>
Effective Date:<Effective date>Approved By: <Name and job title of the executive sponsor>
Last Review:<Date of last review>Next Review: <Date of next review>

Purpose

This analysis shows which services and activities of {{company_name}} matter most, how fast harm grows when they stop, and how quickly each must come back. Its targets drive the Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery Plan, backup settings and recovery tests. It supports ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A controls A.5.29 and A.5.30, SOC 2 criteria CC9.1 and A1.2, and Verity control BC-03.

Scope

Every customer facing service in the ISMS and SOC 2 scope, and the internal activities those services rely on, such as support, billing, deployment, identity and security monitoring.

Roles and Responsibilities

  • Executive sponsor (<Name and job title of the executive sponsor>): approves the ratings, the targets and the insurance decision, and accepts any gap between a target and what can be achieved.
  • Business continuity owner (<Name and job title of the business continuity owner>): runs the analysis, keeps the tables current and passes the targets into the continuity plan.
  • Service owners: rate the impact for their service, name its dependencies and confirm the targets.
  • Engineering lead: confirms what the architecture, backups and redundancy can actually achieve, using the latest test results.

1. When the Analysis Is Done

  1. At least once a year, before the yearly review of the continuity plan.
  2. Before a new service goes live, and after a major change to architecture, hosting region, a key supplier or a customer commitment.
  3. After a real disruption that showed a rating or a target was wrong.

2. Method

  1. List the services and activities from Assets and the SOC 2 System Description.
  2. For each one, rate the impact at each time point in section 3 for five kinds of harm: customers, contracts and money, legal and regulatory duties, reputation, and the safety of information.
  3. Set the maximum tolerable outage: the time after which the harm becomes severe.
  4. Set the recovery time objective (RTO) shorter than the maximum tolerable outage, the recovery point objective (RPO) from how much lost data customers and contracts can bear, and the minimum service level to run during a disruption.
  5. Name every dependency: people and skills, systems, data, suppliers and sites.
  6. Compare each target with the commitments in contracts and service level agreements. A target looser than a commitment is a gap.
  7. The engineering lead checks each target against the last recovery test. A target that cannot be met is raised as a risk in the Risk register.

3. Impact Scale

Rate each service at these time points: <Time points for rating, for example 1 hour, 4 hours, 1 day, 3 days and 1 week>.

RatingWhat it means
1 LowInconvenience. Few customers notice and no contract is breached.
2 ModerateSome customers affected, service credits possible, extra effort to catch up.
3 HighMany customers affected, service levels missed, complaints, a regulator or a major customer may ask questions, or lost revenue above <Revenue loss that counts as high, for example one percent of monthly revenue>.
4 SevereCustomers lose data or cannot work, contracts are breached, notification duties start, or trust and revenue suffer lasting harm.

4. Impact and Recovery Targets

Add a row for each service or activity.

Service or activityOwnerRating at each time pointMaximum tolerable outageRTORPOMinimum service level
<Service or activity><Service owner><Ratings at each time point, for example 1, 2, 3, 4, 4><Maximum tolerable outage><Recovery time objective><Recovery point objective><Minimum service level during a disruption>

5. Dependencies

  1. Every single point of failure is listed, including a person whose knowledge nobody else has.
  2. Supplier dependencies match Vendors. The vendor owner compares each supplier's own recovery commitments with the targets in section 4 and raises a gap as a risk.
  3. Each workaround keeps the security controls the service relies on, such as access control, logging and encryption. If a workaround needs a control relaxed, the plan names who may approve that, what compensates and when it ends.
Service or activityPeople and skillsSystems and dataSuppliersSites or regionsWorkaround if lost
<Service or activity><Key people or skills, and who covers for them><Systems and data it needs><Suppliers it depends on><Sites or cloud regions><Workaround that keeps the security controls in place>

6. Can the Technology Meet the Targets

  1. For each target, the engineering lead records how the technology meets it: redundancy, backups and the failover method.
  2. Backup frequency must meet the RPO (control BC-01). Restore tests measure recovery time against the RTO (control BC-02).
  3. The result of the last test is entered next to each target. A target not met is a risk with an owner and a treatment.
Service or activityRedundancyBackup frequencyLast testRecovery time achievedTarget met
<Service or activity><Redundancy, for example two availability zones and a standby region><Backup frequency><Date of the last recovery test><Recovery time achieved in the test><Yes or no>

7. Disruption Risks and Insurance

  1. These disruption scenarios are assessed in the Risk register and linked to the services they affect: loss of a cloud region, loss of a key supplier, ransomware or another destructive attack, loss of key people, and loss of office or internet access.
  2. Once a year the executive sponsor decides whether to buy or keep insurance against disruption and security incidents, and records the cover, the limits, the main exclusions and the reason. A decision not to insure is recorded as well.
InsuranceDecision and reasonCover and limitRenewal date
<Type of insurance, for example cyber or business interruption><Held, not held or under review, with the reason><Cover and limit><Renewal date>

8. Approval and Use

  1. The executive sponsor approves each version through the approval tiers in Documents.
  2. Within <Number of days to update the continuity plan after the analysis> days of approval, the business continuity owner updates the continuity plan with the new targets and dependencies.
  3. Sales and legal do not promise customers a recovery time or data loss limit tighter than the approved targets.

Records and Evidence

RecordWhere it is kept in Verity
Approved analysis, every versionDocuments, with approvals; attached as evidence to control BC-03
Recovery test results against the targetsEvidence on BC-02 and the exercise or test report on BC-03
Disruption risks and gapsRisk register
Insurance decisionAttached as evidence to BC-03 with the approval date

Exceptions

A target that cannot be met is allowed only while it is in the Risk register with an owner and a treatment, and any acceptance by the executive sponsor expires within <Maximum length of an accepted recovery gap, for example six months>.

Review

The business continuity owner reviews this analysis at least once a year and after any trigger in section 1. A review that changes nothing is still recorded.

Related Documents

  • Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery Plan
  • Risk Assessment and Treatment Methodology
  • SOC 2 System Description
  • Third-Party Management Policy
  • Operations Security Policy

title: Infrastructure Security Standard
summary: Minimum technical settings for production: hardening and drift, networks, encryption and keys, secrets, logs and alerts, clocks and session limits, with the record each leaves.
content_html:
Infrastructure Security Standard

Document Type: Standard

Company Name:{{company_name}}
Document Owner:<Name and job title of the engineering lead>Version: <Version number, for example 1.0>
Effective Date:<Effective date>Approved By: <Name and job title of the approver>
Last Review:<Date of last review>Next Review: <Date of next review>

Purpose

This standard sets the minimum technical settings for the infrastructure that runs {{company_name}} services, so engineers build to one standard and drift can be found and fixed. It supports ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A controls A.8.9, A.8.15 to A.8.17, A.8.20 to A.8.22 and A.8.24, SOC 2 criteria CC6.1, CC6.6, CC6.7, CC7.1 and CC7.2, and Verity controls NS-01 to NS-09, NS-11, NS-12, LM-02, LM-03, LM-09 and IAM-11.

Scope

Production and every other environment that holds customer data: cloud accounts, networks, servers, containers, databases, managed services and network devices, plus the identity provider settings that govern sessions. Development and test environments meet sections 1, 2 and 4 and hold no customer data.

Roles and Responsibilities

  • Engineering lead (<Name and job title of the engineering lead>): owns this standard and approves deviations.
  • Platform engineers: build and change infrastructure to this standard, through code wherever possible.
  • Security lead: runs the monitoring, handles alerts and runs the reviews in this standard.
  • System owners: fix findings on their systems inside the timeframes set here.

1. Configuration Baselines

  1. Each type of system, such as operating systems, container images, databases, cloud services and network devices, has a baseline built from <Hardening benchmark, for example CIS Benchmarks>, kept in code or in Documents.
  2. Baselines are built into images and infrastructure code so new systems start hardened. Services, ports, accounts and tools a system does not need are removed or turned off.
  3. Manual changes in a production console are allowed only in an emergency. They are recorded and copied back into code within <Number of business days to copy an emergency change back into code>.
  4. Drift is watched continuously by <Configuration monitoring tool, for example the cloud provider's configuration service>. High risk regressions, such as public storage, logging turned off, an opened management port or encryption turned off, alert at once and are fixed within <Time to fix a high risk configuration regression, for example 24 hours>.
  5. A deviation from a baseline needs the engineering lead's approval with a reason and an end date. Baselines are reviewed yearly and when a new benchmark version is released.

2. Networks

  1. Production, staging, development and corporate networks are separate. Databases and internal services sit in private subnets with no route from the internet.
  2. Inbound traffic is denied by default. Every allow rule has an owner and a purpose, recorded in <Where the firewall rule register is kept, for example comments in the infrastructure code>.
  3. Management ports, such as SSH, RDP and database ports, are never reachable from the internet. Administrators reach systems through <Approved remote access method, for example a zero trust proxy or session manager> with multi factor authentication, per application, and every session is logged.
  4. Network services bought from providers, such as DNS, content delivery and connectivity, have their security features and service levels agreed in the contract and checked at the supplier review.
  5. The rules between network zones are reviewed quarterly and stale rules removed. Separation is tested by trying to reach what should be blocked, at least yearly and after any change to the rules between zones.
  6. The network diagram shows zones, allowed paths and where customer data flows. It is updated with each change and reviewed yearly.
  7. The external attack surface is scanned <External scan frequency, for example weekly> for exposed management ports and unexpected services.

3. Encryption and Keys

SettingMinimum
Data at restEncrypted on every data store, including databases, object storage, snapshots, backups and disks
Keys for data at rest<Key type, for example provider managed keys, or customer managed keys where a contract asks for them>
Data in transit, externalTLS <Minimum TLS version, for example 1.2> or higher, legacy protocols and weak ciphers off, HTTP redirected to HTTPS with HSTS
Data in transit, internalTLS for traffic between services and for database connections
CertificatesExpiry monitored and renewal automated
  1. Keys are held in <Key management service> apart from the data they protect. The right to use a key and the right to manage it are held by different roles.
  2. Keys rotate <Key rotation period, for example yearly> and at once if compromise is suspected. A retired key is disabled first and destroyed only once no data or backup depends on it. Each step is recorded.
  3. Who can use and manage keys is reviewed yearly. Unusual volumes of decrypt calls raise an alert.
  4. Creating an unencrypted data store is blocked by policy, or raises an alert where blocking is not possible.

4. Secrets

  1. Passwords, API keys, tokens and private keys are stored only in <Secrets manager>. They are never kept in source control, images or environment files in a repository.
  2. Secrets are injected at run time. Access is scoped to each service and logged.
  3. Secrets rotate <Secret rotation period, for example every 12 months> and at once when exposed. An exposed secret is handled under the Engineering Security Standard and treated as an incident.

5. Logs, Detection and Alerts

  1. These events are logged: sign in, changes to access, administrator actions, application audit events, cloud control plane activity, network flows where available, and security tool findings.
  2. Logs go to <Central logging platform> and are kept for at least <Log retention period, for example 12 months>, with the most recent three months searchable at once.
  3. Logs are protected against change. The administrators of a system cannot alter or delete its logs. Secrets and personal data are kept out of logs wherever possible.
  4. A log source that stops sending raises an alert.
  5. <Threat detection service> is turned on in every account and region, and its findings go to the on call engineer.
  6. Alerts are few and high signal: failed and unusual sign ins, privilege escalation, unusual outbound traffic, changes to critical files, service outages, resource exhaustion, and detection or logging being turned off. Each alert has an owner and a first response step.
  7. Security events are reviewed at least daily, by alert rules or by a person. Alert volume and false alarms are reviewed quarterly and every tuning decision is recorded.
  8. Confirmed security events are handled under the Incident Response Plan.

6. Clocks and Time Sources

  1. Systems take time only from <Trusted time sources, for example the cloud provider's time service>. Changing time settings is restricted and logged.
  2. Log timestamps use UTC or carry an explicit offset.
  3. The largest clock offset allowed is <Largest clock offset allowed, for example one second>. A larger offset raises an alert, and a sample of systems is checked quarterly.

7. Session Limits

SessionIdle timeoutMaximum length
Staff sign in to the identity provider<Staff idle timeout, for example 30 minutes><Staff session length, for example 12 hours>
Administrative consoles and production access<Administrator idle timeout, for example 15 minutes><Administrator session length, for example 8 hours>
Customer sessions in the product<Customer idle timeout><Customer session length>
  1. A fresh sign in is required before high risk actions, such as changing multi factor settings, granting access or viewing secrets.
  2. Signing out and removing a user end their active sessions and refresh tokens, not only future sign ins.

Records and Evidence

RecordControlsWhere it is kept in Verity
This standard, as the encryption, key, secrets, hardening, remote access, logging, alerting and session standardNS-01, NS-02, NS-04, NS-06, NS-09, NS-11, LM-02, LM-09, IAM-11Documents; attached as evidence to each control
Approved configuration baseline and the drift alerts investigatedLM-03Evidence on LM-03
Approved deviations and exposed management access exceptionsNS-04, NS-08Evidence on each control
Firewall rule register and quarterly rule reviewNS-03Evidence on NS-03
Network diagram, zone rule review and separation test resultsNS-07Evidence on NS-07
Key access review and rotation recordsNS-06Evidence on NS-06
Threat detection alerts that were investigatedNS-05Evidence on NS-05, with the response steps in section 5
Log review and alert tuning reviewLM-02, LM-09Evidence on each control
Time sources and quarterly clock checkNS-12Evidence on NS-12

Exceptions

An exception needs the engineering lead's approval, a reason, a compensating measure and an end date no more than <Maximum length of an exception, for example 90 days> away. An exception that must last longer goes into the Risk register.

Review

The engineering lead reviews this standard at least once a year, and after a major change of architecture, a new hosting provider or a significant incident.

Related Documents

  • Operations Security Policy
  • Cryptography Policy
  • Cloud Services Security Policy
  • Access Control Policy
  • Engineering Security Standard
  • Endpoint Security Standard
  • Incident Response Plan
  • Change Management Procedure

title: Engineering Security Standard
summary: The settings and timeframes engineers work to: who can reach the code, peer review, automated tests, dependency, licence and secret scanning, input checks, security testing and controlled releases.
content_html:
Engineering Security Standard

Document Type: Standard

Company Name:{{company_name}}
Document Owner:<Name and job title of the engineering lead>Version: <Version number, for example 1.0>
Effective Date:<Effective date>Approved By: <Name and job title of the approver>
Last Review:<Date of last review>Next Review: <Date of next review>

Purpose

The Secure Development Policy says what must happen when {{company_name}} builds software. This standard says exactly how: the settings, the tools and the timeframes. It supports ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A controls A.5.32, A.8.4, A.8.25, A.8.28 and A.8.29, SOC 2 criteria CC7.1, CC8.1 and PI1.2, and Verity controls SD-02, SD-03, SD-05, SD-06, SD-11 and SD-13.

Scope

Every repository that holds application code, infrastructure code or configuration for services in scope, the build and deployment pipelines, and the package and image registries. It applies to employees, contractors and outsourced developers. Contracts with outsourced developers require it.

Roles and Responsibilities

  • Engineering lead (<Name and job title of the engineering lead>): owns this standard, approves exceptions and reviews administrator overrides.
  • Engineers: follow this standard in every change they write or review.
  • Security lead: runs the scanning tools, oversees triage and arranges security testing.
  • Repository owners: keep the protection settings on their repositories as set here.

1. Who Can Reach the Code

  1. Code is kept in <Source control platform>. Each repository has a named owner.
  2. Access is through single sign on with multi factor authentication and is granted by team membership. Write access to production repositories is limited to engineers who need it. Administrators are few, listed, and reviewed each quarter in the access review.
  3. A leaver loses access on their last day under the Joiner, Mover and Leaver Checklists.
  4. Forking to personal accounts is blocked. Making a repository public needs the engineering lead's approval.

2. Peer Review and Branch Protection

  1. The default branch of every production repository is protected: no direct pushes, a pull request is required, at least <Number of approving reviews, for example one> approval from someone other than the author, all status checks must pass, authors cannot approve their own change, and approvals are dismissed when new commits arrive.
  2. Reviewers check correctness, tests and security, including access checks, input handling, secrets, and personal data in logs.
  3. Every administrator override is logged and reviewed by the engineering lead <Frequency of override review, for example monthly>.

3. Automated Tests

  1. The test suite runs on every pull request and must pass before merge. Branch protection enforces this.
  2. Where a system processes customer data, tests check the accuracy and completeness of that processing against its specification.
  3. Build results are kept for <Build result retention period, for example 12 months>.
  4. A flaky test is fixed or set aside with a task to fix it. Tests are never skipped silently.

4. Dependencies, Images and Licences

  1. <Dependency scanning tool> scans every repository and image registry. A build fails when a change adds a critical vulnerability.
  2. Findings are triaged and fixed, or a decision recorded, within these timeframes:
SeverityFix or decision within
Critical, or exploited in the wild<Days to fix a critical dependency finding, for example 7> days
High<Days to fix a high dependency finding, for example 30> days
Medium<Days to fix a medium dependency finding, for example 90> days
LowThe next planned update
  1. Each release has a software bill of materials that records every component and its licence.
  2. Components under <Licences allowed without review, for example MIT, Apache 2.0 and BSD> may be used freely. Any other licence is reviewed by <Person who approves other licences> before use. Code copied from elsewhere keeps its notices, and software is used only within the terms it was licensed under.

5. Secrets in Code

  1. Secret scanning runs on every repository, including its full history, and blocks pushes that contain a secret.
  2. Engineers use the pre commit hook that checks for secrets.
  3. When a secret is exposed, the owner rotates it at once, checks the logs for use before rotation, records the rotation, and reports the exposure as a security incident. Reverting the commit is never enough.

6. Coding Rules and Input Handling

  1. Engineers follow <Secure coding guide, for example the OWASP Top 10 and the team's language guides>.
  2. Every input that crosses a boundary is checked against its schema, type, range and required fields. Invalid input is rejected with an error or sent to a monitored queue, never dropped silently. Duplicate submissions are detected.
  3. A rejection rate above <Rejection rate that raises an alert, for example two percent of requests> raises an alert, because it points to a fault upstream.
  4. Queries are parameterized, output is encoded for where it is shown, access is checked on the server, and no code is built from user input.
  5. Developers complete secure coding training at joining and every year after.

7. Testing for Security Before Release

  1. Static analysis by <Static analysis tool> runs on every pull request.
  2. A new externally facing feature or a major release gets a security design review and <Dynamic testing before release, for example an authenticated scan of the staging environment>.
  3. An independent penetration test runs every year and after a major change. Its findings are tracked in Vulnerabilities.
  4. A release ships with no open critical or high finding from these tests unless an exception is approved.

8. Releases to Production

  1. Production is deployed only from the protected default branch or from a release the pipeline built.
  2. A production deployment needs an approval or a protected environment with named reviewers: <Who may approve production deployments>.
  3. Deployment credentials live in the pipeline, never on laptops. Only the pipeline and named people can deploy.
  4. The deployment history records what was released, from which commit, when, by whom and who approved it.
  5. Emergency releases follow the emergency path in the Change Management Procedure.

Records and Evidence

RecordControlsWhere it is kept in Verity
This standard, as the testing, triage, input checking, peer review, secret rotation and deployment standardSD-02, SD-03, SD-05, SD-06, SD-11, SD-13Documents; attached as evidence to each control
Test run results for the changes in the periodSD-02Evidence on SD-02, or from the source control connector
Dependency alerts triaged inside the timeframesSD-03Evidence on SD-03
Record that input checks were testedSD-05Evidence on SD-05
List of reviewed changes and the override reviewSD-06Evidence on SD-06
Rotation records for exposed secretsSD-11Evidence on SD-11
Deployment history with commit, approver and timeSD-13Evidence on SD-13

Exceptions

An exception needs the engineering lead's approval with a reason, a compensating measure and an end date. A missed fix timeframe is either fixed or recorded as an accepted risk in Vulnerabilities.

Review

The engineering lead reviews this standard at least once a year, and after a change of tools, a significant incident, or a penetration test that finds a pattern of weakness.

Related Documents

  • Secure Development Policy
  • Change Management Procedure
  • Infrastructure Security Standard
  • Processing Integrity Procedure and Specifications
  • Joiner, Mover and Leaver Checklists

title: Endpoint Security Standard
summary: Settings every laptop, desktop and phone must meet before it touches company data: enrolment, encryption, screen lock, updates, malware detection, lost devices and care away from the office.
content_html:
Endpoint Security Standard

Document Type: Standard

Company Name:{{company_name}}
Document Owner:<Name and job title of the IT lead>Version: <Version number, for example 1.0>
Effective Date:<Effective date>Approved By: <Name and job title of the approver>
Last Review:<Date of last review>Next Review: <Date of next review>

Purpose

This standard sets the settings every device must meet before it reaches {{company_name}} data, and how those settings are checked. It supports ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A controls A.7.9, A.8.1 and A.8.7, SOC 2 criteria CC6.5, CC6.7 and CC6.8, and Verity controls EP-01 to EP-06.

Scope

Company laptops, desktops, tablets and phones, and any personal device that section 1 allows to reach company data. Servers are covered by the Infrastructure Security Standard.

Roles and Responsibilities

  • IT lead (<Name and job title of the IT lead>): owns this standard, runs device management and reports compliance.
  • Staff and contractors: keep their devices compliant, never turn off a setting, and report a lost device at once.
  • Security lead: handles malware detections and approves exceptions with the IT lead.

1. Enrolment and Inventory

  1. Every company device is enrolled in <Device management tool> before it is issued.
  2. The inventory records the owner, serial number, model, operating system, encryption status and last check in. Each device is also recorded in Assets.
  3. The IT lead reconciles enrolled devices with the staff list <Device reconciliation frequency, for example quarterly>. An unmanaged device found is enrolled or blocked.
  4. Personal devices: <Personal device rule, for example not allowed, or allowed for email and chat only when enrolled in the mobile management profile>.

2. Required Settings

SettingRequirementControl
Full disk encryptionOn, with the recovery key held in device managementEP-02
Screen lockLocks after <Screen lock idle time, for example 5 minutes> idle, never more than 15 minutes, and needs a password or biometric to unlockEP-06
Operating system and browser updatesAutomatic, inside the timeframes in section 3EP-04
Malware detection<Endpoint protection product> installed, healthy and updating itselfEP-01
Local firewallOnEP-03
Administrator rightsNo standing local administrator rights. Elevation through <How users get administrator rights when needed>EP-03
Sign inCompany identity account with multi factor authenticationEP-03
Removable media<Removable media rule, for example blocked, or allowed only when scanned on connection and encrypted>EP-01

A device that fails a setting is marked out of compliance, loses access to company applications where device checks allow it, and is fixed within <Days to fix an out of compliance device, for example 5 business days>.

3. Updates

UpdateInstalled within
Critical, or exploited in the wild<Time to install a critical update, for example 72 hours>
High<Time to install a high update, for example 14 days>
Other<Time to install other updates, for example 30 days>
  1. Device management pushes updates. Staff do not have to act, except to restart when asked.
  2. A device on an operating system version its maker no longer supports is upgraded or replaced.
  3. The IT lead runs a compliance report each month and follows up every device outside the timeframe.

4. Malware Detection

  1. Detections go to <Where detections are sent, for example the security alert channel and the on call engineer> and are handled under the Incident Response Plan.
  2. A device without a healthy agent is an exception to resolve, not a normal state.
  3. The security lead reviews the detections acted on each quarter.

5. Lost, Stolen and Returned Devices

  1. Staff report a lost or stolen device at once through <Security reporting channel, for example a security email address or chat channel>.
  2. The IT lead locks and wipes the device, keeps the wipe confirmation, and treats the loss as a security event. If the device never reconnects, the passwords, sessions and tokens it held are revoked.
  3. Leavers return devices on their last day. A device not returned within <Days allowed to return a device after leaving, for example 5 business days> is wiped remotely.
  4. A device is wiped and rebuilt before it is given to someone else. Disposal follows the Data Management Policy, with a destruction record for each serial number.

6. Devices Away From the Office

  1. Devices are never left unattended in public places or in view in a vehicle.
  2. Staff use a privacy screen where others can see the display, and lock the screen whenever they step away.
  3. Devices travel as hand luggage and connect only through trusted networks or the company remote access method.

[Optional] For travel to countries named in <Where the list of high risk destinations is kept>, staff take a loan device with minimal data, and the IT lead rebuilds it on return.

7. Compliance Monitoring

  1. The IT lead checks the device management dashboard every week and fixes failures.
  2. Each month the IT lead attaches the patch compliance report to control EP-04, and each quarter the device inventory to control EP-03.
  3. Compliance results are reported to management review.

Records and Evidence

RecordControlsWhere it is kept in Verity
This standard, as the endpoint protection, encryption, device management, patch and screen lock standardEP-01, EP-02, EP-03, EP-04, EP-06Documents; attached as evidence to each control
Section 5, as the lost device and leaver procedureEP-05Documents; attached as evidence to EP-05
Detections reviewed and acted onEP-01Evidence on EP-01, quarterly
Approved encryption exceptionsEP-02Evidence on EP-02
Device inventoryEP-03Assets, and evidence on EP-03, quarterly
Patch compliance reportEP-04Evidence on EP-04, monthly
Wipe confirmationsEP-05Evidence on EP-05, for each event

Exceptions

An exception needs approval by the IT lead and the security lead, a compensating measure, and an end date no more than <Maximum length of a device exception, for example 90 days> away. Each exception is recorded as evidence on the control it affects.

Review

The IT lead reviews this standard at least once a year, and after a change of device management or endpoint protection tools, or a significant device related incident.

Related Documents

  • Acceptable Use Policy
  • Remote Working Policy
  • Asset Management Policy
  • Joiner, Mover and Leaver Checklists
  • Incident Response Plan
  • Data Management Policy

title: Joiner, Mover and Leaver Checklists
summary: Checklists for people joining, changing role and leaving, contractors included: agreements, training, access granted and removed on time, assets returned, duties handed over, each item recorded.
content_html:
Joiner, Mover and Leaver Checklists

Document Type: Procedure

Company Name:{{company_name}}
Document Owner:<Name and job title of the people operations lead>Version: <Version number, for example 1.0>
Effective Date:<Effective date>Approved By: <Name and job title of the approver>
Last Review:<Date of last review>Next Review: <Date of next review>

Purpose

These checklists make sure that everyone who joins, changes role or leaves {{company_name}} gets exactly the access they need, no more, and that access, devices and duties are handed back on time. Each item leaves a record. They support ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A controls A.5.11, A.5.16, A.5.18 and A.6.5, SOC 2 criteria CC6.2 and CC6.3, and Verity controls HR-03, HR-05, HR-06 and IAM-12.

Scope

Employees, contractors, interns, temporary staff and individuals from suppliers who have access to {{company_name}} systems, data or premises.

Roles and Responsibilities

  • People operations lead (<Name and job title of the people operations lead>): owns these checklists, starts each one from the HR record and runs the quarterly roster check.
  • Hiring or line manager: chooses the role, approves access needs and hands over duties.
  • IT lead: creates and removes accounts, issues and recovers devices.
  • System owners: grant and remove access in systems outside single sign on.
  • Security lead: approves privileged access, verifies every leaver checklist and rotates shared secrets.
  • Contractor sponsor: the employee accountable for each contractor's access and end date.

1. Triggers and Deadlines

EventTriggerDeadline
JoinerSigned contract recorded in <HR system>Checklist complete within <Days after the start date to complete the joiner checklist, for example 5 business days>; security training within <Days to complete security training, for example 30 days>
MoverRole change recorded in the HR systemAccess no longer needed removed within <Days to remove access after a role change, for example 5 business days>
Planned leaverResignation or end date recordedAll access removed by the end of the last working day
Involuntary leaverDecision to end employmentAll access removed within <Hours to remove access after an involuntary departure, for example 2 hours> of the decision, and before the person is told where possible
Contractor endEnd date in the contractor registerAccess ends on the end date unless the sponsor extends it in writing
  1. Each event opens a task in Tasks titled with the event and the person's name, for example "Leaver: Sam Lee", with the checklist below attached.
  2. Each item is marked by the person who did it, with the date. An item that does not apply is marked so, with the reason.
  3. The task closes only when every item is complete. The security lead verifies every leaver task before it closes.

2. Joiner Checklist

ItemOwnerRecord
Identity and right to work checked, and background check done to the level set for the rolePeople operationsScreening result (HR-01)
Confidentiality and intellectual property agreement signedPeople operationsSigned agreement (HR-02)
Role chosen from the role and access matrix, never copied from another userHiring managerApproved access request in <Access request system> (IAM-01)
Identity account created and multi factor authentication set up at first sign inITIdentity provider record
Device issued, enrolled in device management and recorded in Assets with the person as ownerITAsset record
Security policy, acceptable use policy and code of conduct acknowledgedJoinerAcknowledgement campaign in Documents (CS-04)
Security awareness training completedJoinerTraining record (HR-08)
Security duties of the role explained and stated in the job descriptionHiring managerJob description (HR-04)
Privileged or production access, if needed, approved separatelySecurity leadApproval record (IAM-07)

3. Mover Checklist

ItemOwnerRecord
Access needed for the new role requested and approvedNew managerApproved access request (IAM-01)
Access not needed in the new role removed, not kept just in casePrevious manager and system ownersRemoval record
New access checked against the conflicting duties matrixSecurity leadReview note (IAM-09)
Duties held in the old role reassigned, such as on call, approvals, shared accounts and key custodyPrevious managerTask note
Devices and other assets not needed returned or reassigned in AssetsITAsset record
Training the new role needs assigned, such as secure codingNew managerTraining record
Ownership of documents, controls, risks and tasks in Verity moved to the right personPrevious managerVerity audit log

4. Leaver Checklist

ItemOwnerRecord
Identity account disabled, and active sessions and tokens revokedITIdentity provider log
Access removed in systems outside single sign on: <Systems outside single sign on that need manual removal>System ownersRemoval record for each system
Source control, cloud console, remote access and Verity membership removedITRemoval record
Shared passwords and secrets the person knew rotated, and any code or combination they knew changedSecurity leadRotation record
Laptop, phone, hardware tokens, badges and keys returned, or the device wiped remotelyITAsset record and wipe confirmation (EP-05)
Ownership of documents, accounts, controls, risks and tasks moved to a named personLine managerVerity audit log
Written reminder of the duties that continue after leaving, such as confidentiality, acknowledged by the leaverPeople operationsSigned reminder
Final check that no active account remains in the identity provider or the systems listed aboveSecurity leadVerification note on the task

5. Contractors

  1. Every contractor is in the contractor register in <Where the contractor register is kept, for example Vendors or the HR system>, with the sponsor, their firm, the scope of access, a start date and a mandatory end date.
  2. Contractors complete the joiner checklist. Where they work through a firm, the firm's contract carries the confidentiality terms.
  3. Access ends on the end date. Extending it needs the sponsor to act and record a new end date. Silence never extends access.
  4. Contractors are included in every access review.

6. Checks

  1. Each quarter, people operations produces the roster of joiners, movers and leavers with dates. The security lead compares it with the identity provider and the removal records, investigates every account without a current owner, and raises each late removal as an issue.
  2. The share of leavers whose access was removed by the deadline is reported to management review.

Records and Evidence

RecordControlsWhere it is kept in Verity
Section 2, as the onboarding checklistHR-06Documents; attached as evidence to HR-06
Completed joiner tasksHR-06Tasks, and evidence on HR-06 for each joiner
Section 4, as the offboarding checklist, and section 1, as the access removal procedure with its timeframeHR-05, IAM-12Documents; attached as evidence to each control
Completed leaver tasks and removal recordsHR-05, IAM-12Tasks, and evidence on each control for each leaver
Quarterly roster of joiners and leaversHR-05Evidence on HR-05
Section 5, as the contractor procedure, and the contractor registerHR-03Documents and evidence on HR-03, quarterly

Records are kept for <Retention period for people records, for example the length of employment plus three years>.

Exceptions

A deadline may be missed only with the security lead's approval, recorded on the task with the reason. Access of an involuntary leaver is never kept beyond the deadline.

Review

The people operations lead reviews these checklists at least once a year, and after a late removal, a new HR or identity system, or a change to the role and access matrix.

Related Documents

  • Human Resource Security Policy
  • Access Control Policy
  • Endpoint Security Standard
  • Asset Management Policy
  • Code of Conduct

title: Privacy Notice Outline
summary: Outline of the public privacy notice: who is responsible, what is collected and why, sharing, transfers, retention, rights and contacts, with the checks to run before each version is published.
content_html:
Privacy Notice Outline

Document Type: Policy

Company Name:{{company_name}}
Document Owner:<Name and job title of the privacy lead>Version: <Version number, for example 1.0>
Effective Date:<Effective date>Approved By: <Name and job title of the approver>
Last Review:<Date of last review>Next Review: <Date of next review>

Purpose

This outline is the starting point for the privacy notice that {{company_name}} publishes. The notice tells people what personal data {{company_name}} holds about them, why, who sees it, how long it is kept and what they can do about it. Every other privacy control is judged against it. It supports ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A control A.5.34, SOC 2 criterion P1.1 and Verity control DM-15.

Roles and Responsibilities

  • Privacy lead (<Name and job title of the privacy lead>): owns the notice, keeps it true to practice and runs the yearly check.
  • Privacy counsel: confirms which laws apply and that the notice meets them, before first publication and after each material change.
  • Product and engineering leads: tell the privacy lead before any new collection, purpose, recipient or transfer.

Using This Outline

This section is internal. Remove it before publishing.

  1. Write the notice from the data inventory and data map (control DM-06) and the purpose register in the Personal Data Handling Procedure. Never copy another company's notice.
  2. Use plain words and short sentences. Put the most important points first.
  3. Sections marked [Optional] apply only in some cases. Remove those that do not apply to {{company_name}}.
  4. Where {{company_name}} processes personal data inside customer content only on its customers' instructions, this notice covers only the data {{company_name}} itself decides about, such as website visitors, customer account contacts and job applicants. Say that each customer's own notice covers its end users.
  5. Give each published notice a version and an effective date, and keep every earlier version in Documents.
  6. Tell people about a material change through <Channel used to tell people about material changes, for example email to account owners and a banner on the website> before it takes effect.
  7. Once a year, check a sample of collection points, recipients and retention periods against what the notice says.

Notice Outline

1. Who We Are

{{company_name}}, <Legal entity name and registered address>, is responsible for the personal data described in this notice. You can reach us about privacy at <Privacy contact email address or web form>.

[Optional] Our data protection officer is <Name or role and contact details of the data protection officer>.

[Optional] Our representative is <Name and contact details of the local representative, where one is required>.

2. What This Notice Covers

This notice covers personal data about <Groups of people covered, for example website visitors, customer account users, prospects and job applicants>. It does not cover data we process for our customers inside our service. Our customers decide how that data is used, and their own privacy notices apply to it.

3. Personal Data We Collect

CategoryExamplesWhere it comes from
Account and contact detailsName, work email, job title, companyFrom you when you sign up or contact us
Usage and device dataPages viewed, features used, IP address, browser typeFrom your device when you use the website or service
Billing detailsBilling contact, invoices, payment statusFrom you or your employer
CommunicationsSupport requests, emails, call notesFrom you
<Other category of personal data><Examples of the data><Where the data comes from>

[Optional] We do not seek to collect sensitive personal data, such as health or biometric data. Where we do, we say why and ask for explicit consent where the law requires it.

4. Why We Use It

PurposeData usedLegal basis, where the law requires one
Provide and support the serviceAccount, usage and communicationsOur contract with you or your employer
Keep the service secure and prevent abuseUsage and device dataOur legitimate interest in a secure service
Bill for the serviceBilling detailsOur contract, and our legal duty to keep accounts
Send product news and marketingAccount and contact detailsYour consent, or our legitimate interest, and you can opt out at any time
Meet legal dutiesThe data a duty requiresLegal obligation
<Other purpose><Data used for the purpose><Legal basis for the purpose>

We use personal data only for these purposes. Before we use it for a new purpose, we update this notice and, where needed, ask for consent.

[Optional] <Statement on whether personal data is used to train AI models, and how to object>

5. Who We Share It With

  1. Service providers who process data for us, listed at <Where the subprocessor list is published>. Each is bound by a contract that limits how it uses the data.
  2. Professional advisers, such as lawyers and auditors, under a duty of confidentiality.
  3. Authorities, when the law requires it.
  4. A buyer or investor, if {{company_name}} is involved in a merger or sale, under the same protections.

We do not sell personal data.

6. Transfers to Other Countries

[Optional] <Countries the data is transferred to and the safeguard used for each>

7. How Long We Keep It

CategoryHow long we keep it
<Category of personal data><Retention period and what happens to the data after it>

These periods match the retention schedule in the Data Management Policy.

8. How We Protect It

We protect personal data with encryption, access control, staff training and checks on our suppliers. More detail is at <Link to the security or trust page>.

9. Your Rights and Choices

Depending on where you live, you can ask to see your data, correct it, delete it, limit or object to how we use it, receive a copy in a common format, and withdraw consent you gave. You can also complain to a data protection authority.

To make a request, use <How to make a privacy request, for example the privacy request form or email address>. We check who you are before we act, and we reply within <Response time promised, for example one month>. Using your rights will not affect how we treat you.

10. Cookies and Similar Technologies

[Optional] <Link to the cookie notice, or a short description of the cookies used and how to control them>

11. Children

[Optional] Our service is not meant for children under <Minimum age for using the service>, and we do not knowingly collect their data.

12. Changes to This Notice

This notice took effect on <Effective date>. When we change it in a way that matters, we will tell you before the change takes effect.

13. Contact and Complaints

Send questions or complaints to <Privacy contact email address or web form>. If you are not satisfied with our answer, you can contact <Data protection authority or dispute resolution body named for complaints>.

Records and Evidence

RecordWhere it is kept in Verity

Yearly check of the notice against practiceA task in Tasks with the sample checked and the result

Exceptions

None. A practice that differs from the notice is raised as an issue at once, and either the practice or the notice is changed.

Review

The privacy lead reviews the notice at least once a year, and before any new collection, purpose, recipient, transfer or product that it would need to describe.

title: Privacy Requests and Complaints Procedure
summary: How privacy requests, questions and complaints are received, checked, answered on time, passed on to customers and third parties and logged, and how patterns are reviewed.
content_html:
Privacy Requests and Complaints Procedure

Document Type: Procedure

Company Name:{{company_name}}
Document Owner:<Name and job title of the privacy lead>Version: <Version number, for example 1.0>
Effective Date:<Effective date>Approved By: <Name and job title of the approver>
Last Review:<Date of last review>Next Review: <Date of next review>

Purpose

This procedure sets out how {{company_name}} handles requests from people about their personal data, and privacy questions and complaints, so each one is answered correctly and on time and leaves a record. It supports ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A control A.5.34, SOC 2 criteria P5.1, P5.2, P6.7 and P8.1, and Verity controls DM-05, DM-11 and DM-14.

Scope

Requests, questions and complaints from any person about personal data that {{company_name}} decides about. It also covers requests that reach {{company_name}} about data it processes for a customer, which are passed to that customer under section 3.

Roles and Responsibilities

  • Privacy lead (<Name and job title of the privacy lead>): owns this procedure, decides on each request and complaint, and signs off every response.
  • Request handlers: the support team members trained to log, acknowledge and track requests.
  • System owners: search for, export, correct or delete data in their systems when asked, and confirm on the task.
  • Privacy counsel: advises on refusals, extensions and requests that are unclear or disputed.
  • Vendor owners: pass requests on to the service providers who hold the data.

1. Receiving Requests

  1. Requests come in through <Privacy request channels, for example the privacy form, the privacy email address and the account settings page>, as stated in the privacy notice.
  2. A request that arrives anywhere else, such as a support ticket, sales email or social media message, is passed to the privacy queue within <Time to pass on a request received elsewhere, for example one business day>.
  3. Each request is logged as a task in Tasks, tagged privacy request, with the date received, the type, the channel, the deadline and the owner.
  4. The requester gets an acknowledgement within <Days to acknowledge a request, for example 3 business days>.
  5. The deadline runs from the date received: <Response deadline, for example one month, extendable where the law allows for complex requests>.
  6. No fee is charged unless a request is clearly unfounded or excessive and the law allows it. The privacy lead decides and records why.

2. Checking Identity

  1. Identity checks match the risk. Usually, matching the request to the email address or account the data belongs to is enough. Sensitive data needs a stronger check.
  2. Ask only for what is needed to confirm identity. Delete identity documents once the check is done.
  3. A person acting for someone else must show that they are authorized.
  4. If identity cannot be confirmed, tell the requester what is needed. Nothing is disclosed or changed until it is.

3. Requests About Customer Data

When the data belongs to a customer's end users and {{company_name}} only processes it for that customer, the handler does not act on the substance. The request is passed to the customer within <Days to pass a request to the customer, for example 2 business days>, the requester is told, and {{company_name}} helps the customer answer as the data processing agreement requires.

4. Handling Each Type of Request

RequestWhat is doneControl
See my dataGather the data from every system in the data map, with its purposes, sources, recipients and retention. Include the record of disclosures to third parties from the disclosure register.DM-11
Correct my dataCorrect it, pass the correction to the systems and service providers that hold copies within <Days to pass on a correction, for example 5 business days>, and tell third parties who received the old data. If a correction is refused, record the reason and keep the person's statement of disagreement with the data.DM-05
Delete my dataDelete or anonymize it unless a legal reason to keep it applies, and tell service providers. Backups age out on their normal schedule.DM-05
Stop or limit a use, or stop marketingStop the use in every system and tell service providers.DM-11
Give me a copy to take elsewhereExport the data in a common machine readable format.DM-11
Withdraw my consentStop the processing that relied on it and update the consent record, under the Personal Data Handling Procedure.DM-11
  1. The handler uses the data map (control DM-06) as the checklist of systems to search, and records each system searched on the task.
  2. The privacy lead reviews each response before it is sent through a secure channel.
  3. A refusal, in whole or in part, gives the reason, the legal ground and the right to complain. Privacy counsel reviews every refusal before it is sent.

5. Questions and Complaints

  1. Privacy questions and complaints come through the same channels and are logged as tasks tagged privacy complaint, each with an owner.
  2. The owner investigates, fixes the cause and replies with the outcome within <Days to resolve a privacy complaint, for example 30 days>.
  3. The reply tells the person how to take the matter further: <Data protection authority or dispute resolution body named for complaints>.
  4. A complaint that reveals a possible breach is handled at once under the Incident Response Plan.

6. Reviewing Patterns

  1. Each quarter the privacy lead reviews all requests and complaints: numbers by type, the share answered on time, the median time to answer, complaints still open, and repeated causes.
  2. Each systemic cause is raised as an issue under the Corrective Action and Improvement Procedure.
  3. The results go to management review.

Records and Evidence

RecordControlsWhere it is kept in Verity
This procedure, as the access, correction and complaint proceduresDM-11, DM-05, DM-14Documents; attached as evidence to each control
Log of requests with dates and outcomesDM-11Tasks tagged privacy request; export attached to DM-11
Sample responses that include the record of disclosuresDM-11Attached to the request task and to DM-11
Log of corrections and how third parties were toldDM-05Tasks; export attached to DM-05
Log of questions and complaints with resolution timesDM-14Tasks tagged privacy complaint; quarterly export attached to DM-14

Request records are kept for <Retention period for privacy request records, for example three years after closure>. They hold only what is needed to show how each request was handled.

Exceptions

A deadline is extended only where the law allows it. The privacy lead decides, and the requester is told the reason before the first deadline passes.

Review

The privacy lead reviews this procedure at least once a year, and after a change in the law, a complaint upheld by an authority, or a missed deadline.

Related Documents

  • Privacy Notice
  • Personal Data Handling Procedure and Registers
  • Data Management Policy
  • Incident Response Plan
  • Third-Party Management Policy

title: Personal Data Handling Procedure and Registers
summary: How personal data is collected, used, shared and kept accurate inside its stated purposes, with the purpose, consent, disclosure and breach registers the privacy controls ask for.
content_html:
Personal Data Handling Procedure and Registers

Document Type: Procedure

Company Name:{{company_name}}
Document Owner:<Name and job title of the privacy lead>Version: <Version number, for example 1.0>
Effective Date:<Effective date>Approved By: <Name and job title of the approver>
Last Review:<Date of last review>Next Review: <Date of next review>

Purpose

This procedure sets out how {{company_name}} collects, uses, shares and keeps accurate the personal data it holds, so that practice matches the privacy notice. It also defines the registers that show this. It supports ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A control A.5.34, SOC 2 criteria P2.1, P3.1, P3.2, P4.1, P6.1 to P6.3 and P7.1, and Verity controls DM-02, DM-03, DM-07, DM-09 and DM-12.

Scope

All personal data that {{company_name}} decides about. Where {{company_name}} processes personal data for a customer, the customer's instructions in the data processing agreement come first, and those activities are still recorded in the purpose register.

Roles and Responsibilities

  • Privacy lead (<Name and job title of the privacy lead>): owns this procedure and the registers, and approves every new use of personal data.
  • Product and engineering leads: raise a privacy review before building anything that collects, uses or shares personal data in a new way.
  • Data owners: keep the data in their systems accurate and within its purpose.
  • Vendor owners: make sure every service provider that receives personal data is reviewed and under contract.
  • Security lead: records and handles unauthorized disclosures under the Incident Response Plan.

1. Purpose Register

  1. Every processing activity is in the purpose register before it starts. The register is kept in <Where the purpose register is kept, for example a register document in Documents linked to the systems in Assets>.
  2. The privacy lead checks the register against actual data flows at least once a year.
ActivityPurposeData categoriesPeople affectedLegal basis or consentSystemsRecipientsRetentionOwner
<Processing activity><Purpose of the activity><Data categories used><People affected><Legal basis, or the consent relied on><Systems used><Recipients of the data><Retention period><Activity owner>

2. Collecting Only What Is Needed

  1. Each collection point, such as a form, an API field, an import or a tracking tag, is linked to a purpose in the register. A field that serves no purpose is removed.
  2. New fields are questioned at design review. The design document and pull request template ask what personal data is added and why.
  3. Personal data is kept out of logs, error trackers and analytics events, or masked before it gets there.
  4. The privacy lead reviews every collection point once a year and removes fields no longer used.

3. Consent and Choice

  1. At each collection point, people are told what is collected, why, and what happens if they do not provide it, in words that match the privacy notice.
  2. Where consent is the basis, it is asked for separately for each purpose, never pre ticked, never bundled into the terms, and is as easy to withdraw as to give.
  3. Each consent record holds who gave it, when, for what purpose, which notice version was shown and how it was captured. Records are kept in <System that stores consent records>.
  4. Explicit consent is obtained before sensitive data is relied on, where the law requires it.
  5. A withdrawal is applied in every system and passed to service providers within <Days to apply a withdrawal of consent, for example 2 business days>.

4. Using Data Only for Its Purpose

  1. Access to personal data is limited to roles whose purpose needs it, under the Access Control Policy.
  2. A new use of personal data needs a privacy review raised as a task in Tasks, stating the purpose, how it fits the notice, the data needed, the legal basis, the risks and the retention. The privacy lead approves before the use starts.
  3. A use that does not fit the notice waits until the notice is updated and, where needed, consent is obtained.
  4. Position on using customer or personal data to train AI models: <Position on using customer or personal data to train AI models>. It is enforced by <How the position is enforced, for example separate data stores and contract terms with AI providers>.

[Optional] Where the law requires it, higher risk processing, such as large scale processing of sensitive data or new monitoring, has a privacy impact assessment before it starts.

5. Keeping Data Accurate

  1. People can update their own account details in the product or by asking support.
  2. Data owners reconcile personal data across systems at least once a year and fix differences.
  3. Corrections are passed on under the Privacy Requests and Complaints Procedure.

6. Sharing With Third Parties

  1. A new flow of personal data to a third party goes through vendor review in Vendors before any data is sent, and a data processing agreement is signed where the recipient processes data for {{company_name}} (control DM-10).
  2. The disclosure register records each recipient, the data categories, the purpose, the legal basis or consent, the transfer safeguard and the start date. It is kept in <Where the disclosure register is kept, for example on each supplier record in Vendors>.
  3. Each disclosure must match the privacy notice and any consent given.
  4. A request from an authority is checked by privacy counsel, answered with the least data needed, and recorded in the register.
  5. The privacy lead reviews the register at least once a year against the systems that actually send data.

7. Unauthorized Disclosures

  1. Every suspected unauthorized disclosure of personal data is recorded in the incident register in Tasks, tagged privacy, including near misses and events that were contained.
  2. Each entry records the data categories, the number of people affected, the cause, the containment, and the notification decision with its reason, including a decision not to notify, and who made it.
  3. Notification follows the Incident Response Plan and the breach notification procedure (control DM-01). The deadlines that apply are <Notification deadlines that apply, for example 72 hours to the regulator and the contract terms for customers>.
  4. The privacy lead reviews the register each quarter for patterns, and raises each repeated cause as an issue.

8. Yearly Privacy Review

Once a year the privacy lead reviews the registers, collection points, purposes, disclosures, consent records and the unauthorized disclosure entries, reports the result to management review, and raises actions in Tasks.

Records and Evidence

RecordControlsWhere it is kept in Verity
Purpose register and reviews of new usesDM-12Location in section 1; attached as evidence to DM-12 yearly
Review of each collection pointDM-07Evidence on DM-07, yearly
Consent records and withdrawal recordsDM-03Consent system; extracts attached to DM-03
Disclosure register and the basis for each disclosureDM-09Vendors; evidence on DM-09
Register of unauthorized disclosures, including near missesDM-02Incident register in Tasks; export attached to DM-02

Exceptions

No personal data is used outside the register. A temporary gap, such as an activity found during the yearly review, is recorded in the register at once and reviewed by the privacy lead within <Days to review an unregistered activity, for example 10 business days>.

Review

The privacy lead reviews this procedure at least once a year, and after a change in the law, a new product that uses personal data, or an unauthorized disclosure.

Related Documents

  • Privacy Notice
  • Privacy Requests and Complaints Procedure
  • Data Management Policy
  • Access Control Policy
  • Third-Party Management Policy
  • Incident Response Plan
