title: Processing Integrity Procedure and Specifications
summary: For when processing integrity is in scope: how each processing flow is specified, how inputs, processing, outputs and stored data are checked, and how errors are found and fixed.
content_html:
Processing Integrity Procedure and Specifications

Document Type: Procedure

Company Name:{{company_name}}
Document Owner:<Name and job title of the engineering lead>Version: <Version number, for example 1.0>
Effective Date:<Effective date>Approved By: <Name and job title of the approver>
Last Review:<Date of last review>Next Review: <Date of next review>

Purpose

This procedure sets out how {{company_name}} makes sure the processing it does for customers is complete, accurate, on time and authorized, and how it shows that. Use it only when processing integrity is one of the SOC 2 categories in scope. It supports SOC 2 criteria PI1.1 to PI1.5 and Verity controls SD-05, SD-07, SD-08 and SD-09.

Scope

Each processing flow listed in section 1. A flow is in scope when customers rely on its results, such as calculations, transformations, reports, imports, exports or scheduled jobs.

Roles and Responsibilities

  • Engineering lead (<Name and job title of the engineering lead>): owns this procedure and approves specifications.
  • Flow owners: keep the specification of their flow current, review reconciliation results and approve reprocessing.
  • Engineers: build the checks in sections 3 to 6 and the tests that prove them.
  • Support lead: logs every error a customer reports and passes it to the flow owner.

1. Processing Flows in Scope

FlowWhat it doesInputsOutputsOwnerCommitment to customers
<Processing flow, for example invoice calculation or report generation><What the flow does><Inputs and their sources><Outputs and who receives them><Flow owner><Accuracy or timeliness commitment made to customers>

2. Specifications

  1. Each flow has a specification, kept in the repository with the code or in Documents, and versioned so the two never drift apart.
  2. A change to the processing logic updates the specification in the same change. The flow owner approves it, and tests are written against the specification rather than against current behaviour.
  3. Where customers rely on a specification, the relevant parts are published in the product or API documentation.
ElementContent
Inputs<Input data definitions, sources and formats>
Checks on input<Validation rules for each input>
Processing<Calculation or transformation rules>
Outputs<Output definitions, recipients and formats>
Timing<Processing schedule and time limits>
Complete and accurate means<How completeness and accuracy are measured, for example record counts and control totals>
Errors<What happens to records that fail a check>

3. Checks on Input

  1. Every input is checked at the boundary against the specification: schema, type, range, required fields and duplicates.
  2. A record that fails is rejected to a monitored queue with the reason. It is never dropped silently.
  3. A rejection rate above <Rejection rate that raises an alert, for example two percent of records in a run> raises an alert to the flow owner.
  4. Each input batch is logged with its source, time and record count.

4. Checks During Processing

  1. Every scheduled job is monitored for success, failure and failure to start. An alert goes to <Where processing alerts go, for example the on call engineer>.
  2. Each run reconciles record counts and control totals between source and destination.
  3. A break is investigated before any reprocessing. Reprocessing needs the flow owner's approval, recorded on the issue.
  4. Changes to processing follow the Change Management Procedure, and the automated tests check them against the specification.

5. Checks on Output

  1. Outputs are checked against inputs, by counts and totals, before they are released.
  2. Outputs reach only the intended recipients, through access controlled channels.
  3. Outputs are kept as long as the specification and the retention schedule say.
  4. An error a customer reports is logged by support and investigated by the flow owner.

6. Stored Data Between Stages

  1. Data between stages is held in durable, versioned storage, not on temporary local disk.
  2. Integrity checks, such as checksums or record counts, run between stages.
  3. Each stage can be rerun without losing or duplicating records.
  4. Data held between stages is kept no longer than the specification and the retention schedule allow. Backups and restore tests cover the stores that matter (controls BC-01 and BC-02).

7. Errors and Corrections

  1. Each processing error is raised as an issue in Tasks, with a severity based on its effect on customers.
  2. Where an error affects a commitment, customers are told under the Security Communication Plan.
  3. The cause is found and fixed under the Corrective Action and Improvement Procedure.
  4. Each month every flow owner reviews the reconciliation results, integrity check results and errors, and attaches them as evidence to controls SD-08 and SD-07.

Records and Evidence

RecordControlsWhere it is kept in Verity
Specifications for each flow and their review after each changeSD-09Repository or Documents; attached as evidence to SD-09
Section 3 and the specifications, as the input checking standard, and a yearly test of those checksSD-05Documents and evidence on SD-05
Section 4, as the reconciliation procedure, and monthly reconciliation results with how breaks were resolvedSD-08Documents and evidence on SD-08
Storage design for each flow and monthly integrity check resultsSD-07Evidence on SD-07
Processing errors and their fixesSD-08Issues in Tasks

Exceptions

A flow may run without a check only with the engineering lead's approval, a compensating manual check, and an end date no more than <Maximum length of a processing exception, for example 30 days> away.

Review

The engineering lead reviews this procedure at least once a year, and after a new flow is added, a significant processing error, or a change to the commitments made to customers.

title: Security Oversight Body Charter
summary: Charter for the board, committee or executive team that oversees security: members and independence, authority, duties, meetings, written packs, minutes and a yearly self review.
content_html:
Organisation: {{legal_name}}. Executive sponsor: {{executive_sponsor}}.

Security Oversight Body Charter

Document Type: Charter

Company Name:{{company_name}}
Document Owner:<Name and job title of the secretary of the oversight body>Version: <Version number, for example 1.0>
Effective Date:<Effective date>Approved By: <Name and job title of the chair of the oversight body>
Last Review:<Date of last review>Next Review: <Date of next review>

Purpose

This charter sets up the body that oversees the security program of {{company_name}} and holds management to account for it. It works for a board with independent members or for an executive team, using section 7 or section 8. It supports ISO/IEC 27001 clause 5.1, SOC 2 criterion CC1.2 and Verity control GOV-02.

Scope

Information security, privacy and resilience matters for everything inside the ISMS scope and the SOC 2 system.

The oversight body is: <Name of the oversight body, for example the Board, the Risk Committee or the Executive Leadership Team>.

Roles and Responsibilities

  • Chair (<Name and job title of the chair of the oversight body>): runs the meetings, approves the agenda and signs the minutes.
  • Members: read the pack, question management and take the decisions in section 3.
  • Security officer: prepares the pack and reports at each meeting, but does not judge their own work.
  • Secretary (<Name and job title of the secretary of the oversight body>): sends the pack, takes the minutes and files them in Verity.

1. Members

MemberRole on the bodyIndependent of managementSince
<Name and job title of the member><Chair or member><Yes or no, with the reason><Date joined>
  1. The body has at least <Minimum number of members, for example three> members.
  2. A meeting can decide only when <Quorum, for example a majority of members including the chair> is present.
  3. The secretary updates the member table, with each member's independence, whenever membership changes and at least once a year.

2. Authority

The body may ask for any information about the security program, speak to any member of staff, ask for outside advice at the company's cost up to <Spending limit for outside advice without further approval>, and require management to act.

3. Duties

  1. Approve the Information Security Policy Statement and the risk appetite.
  2. Review the state of security, material incidents, risk assessment results, the progress of remediation, internal audit and penetration test results, and the results of external audits and SOC 2 reports.
  3. Question management and ask for evidence. The minutes record the questions asked and the answers given.
  4. Decide on resources and on accepting risks above management's authority.
  5. Oversee legal, regulatory and contractual duties, and contact with regulators.
  6. Confirm that management review takes place and that its actions close.

4. Meetings

  1. The body meets at least <Meeting frequency, for example quarterly>, and never less than once a year. It also meets after a major incident.
  2. Security is a standing item on the agenda.
  3. The secretary sends the agenda and the written pack at least <Days before the meeting to send the pack, for example five business days> before each meeting.
  4. Members declare any conflict of interest at the start. A member with a conflict does not take part in that decision, and the minutes say so.

5. Written Pack

The security officer prepares a written pack for each meeting, never only a verbal update. It covers:

  • Progress against the security objectives.
  • The top risks and changes to the Risk register.
  • Incidents since the last meeting and what was learned.
  • Audit and test findings and their status.
  • Control readiness and overdue actions from Verity.
  • Supplier issues and changes to legal or contract duties.
  • The decisions the body is asked to take.

6. Minutes and Decisions

  1. The minutes record who attended, each item discussed, the questions and challenges raised, the decisions, any risks accepted, resource decisions, and actions with owners and dates.
  2. The body approves the minutes at the next meeting. The secretary attaches the approved minutes and the pack as evidence to control GOV-02 within <Days to file approved minutes, for example ten business days> of approval.
  3. Actions are tracked in Tasks and their status is reviewed at each meeting.

7. [Optional] Board With Independent Members

  1. A member is independent when they have not been employed by {{company_name}} in the last <Years since employment for a member to count as independent, for example three> years, have no material business relationship with it, and are not a close relative of an executive.
  2. At least one independent member has experience of security, technology or risk. Where none does, the body appoints an independent adviser.
  3. The independent members meet without management at least once a year.
  4. Where the board delegates security oversight to a committee, the committee reports to the full board after each meeting.

8. [Optional] Executive Team as the Oversight Body

  1. Where {{company_name}} has no board with independent members, the executive team acts as the oversight body. Its members also run the business, so they are overseeing their own work.
  2. To add challenge from outside management, <Source of independent challenge, for example an outside adviser, an investor director or the internal auditor> attends at least <Number of meetings a year the independent party attends, for example two> meetings a year and reports to the body directly.
  3. Internal audit reports go straight to the body. The security officer may raise a concern directly with <Person or group the security officer can escalate to outside the executive team, for example the investors or an outside adviser>.
  4. The limits of this arrangement are recorded in the Risk register and reviewed when {{company_name}} forms a board. The service auditor decides whether the arrangement shows enough independence, so describe it plainly in the SOC 2 System Description.

9. Yearly Self Review

Once a year the body reviews this charter and its own work: whether it met as planned, received written packs, questioned management, and closed its actions. The result and any changes are recorded in the minutes.

Records and Evidence

RecordWhere it is kept in Verity
This charter, every versionDocuments, with approvals; attached as evidence to control GOV-02
Agendas, packs and approved minutesEvidence on GOV-02, for each meeting
Member table with independenceSection 1 of this charter; attached as evidence to GOV-02 each year
Actions from meetingsTasks

Exceptions

A missed meeting is held within <Days to hold a missed meeting, for example 30 days> and the reason is recorded. Two missed meetings in a row are reported to <Person or group told of missed meetings, for example the investors or the full board>.

Review

The body reviews this charter once a year during its self review, and when its membership or the company's governance changes.

Related Documents

  • Information Security Policy Statement
  • Information Security Roles and Responsibilities Policy
  • Management Review Procedure and Minutes
  • Risk Assessment and Treatment Methodology
  • Internal Audit Procedure and Program
  • SOC 2 System Description

title: Site and Equipment Protection Standard
summary: Only for companies that run their own server rooms, comms cabinets or data centers: hazard assessment, environmental protection, power, cabling, equipment placement, servicing and secure disposal.
content_html:
Site and Equipment Protection Standard

Document Type: Standard

Company Name:{{company_name}}
Document Owner:<Name and job title of the facilities or IT lead>Version: <Version number, for example 1.0>
Effective Date:<Effective date>Approved By: <Name and job title of the approver>
Last Review:<Date of last review>Next Review: <Date of next review>

Purpose

This standard protects the sites and equipment that {{company_name}} runs itself from fire, water, heat, power loss, tampering and careless repair, and makes sure equipment leaves with no data on it. It supports ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A controls A.7.5, A.7.8 and A.7.11 to A.7.14, SOC 2 criterion A1.2 and Verity control PE-03.

When to Use This Standard

  1. Use it when {{company_name}} runs its own server room, comms cabinet, data center or recovery site, or holds network or payment equipment at its own premises.
  2. Do not use it when every system is hosted by a cloud provider and the only offices are in managed buildings. In that case the provider's assurance report reviewed under control PE-01 and the landlord's certificates cover these risks. Record that decision with its reason on the Applicability page in Frameworks.

Scope

Every site listed in section 1, and the equipment, power, cooling and cabling at each.

Roles and Responsibilities

  • Facilities or IT lead (<Name and job title of the facilities or IT lead>): owns this standard, keeps the site register and arranges testing and servicing.
  • Site owners: run the yearly hazard assessment for their site and fix what it finds.
  • Security lead: controls access to secure areas and reviews the records each year.
  • Approved engineers: service equipment and protections at the sites, under supervision.
  • Executive sponsor: accepts any risk that remains after the protections are in place.

1. Site Register

SiteAddressTypeEquipment heldSite ownerLast hazard assessment
<Site name><Site address><Site type, for example server room, comms cabinet, data center or recovery site><Equipment held at the site><Site owner><Date of the last hazard assessment>

Each item of equipment is recorded in Assets with its site.

2. Hazard Assessment

  1. Each site owner assesses the site at least once a year and after any change to it, using the method in the Risk Assessment and Treatment Methodology.
  2. The assessment covers fire, water from pipes, roofs or flooding, heat and humidity, power loss, tampering and deliberate damage, risks from neighbours such as kitchens or workshops, and natural events common in the region.
  3. Each hazard is matched to the protections in sections 3 to 6. A risk that remains is recorded in the Risk register with an owner.

3. Environmental Protection

HazardMinimum protectionTest or check
FireDetection linked to a monitored alarm, and suppression suited to electrical equipment, such as a gas system or extinguishers rated for electrical firesYearly, by an approved engineer
WaterWater sensors near equipment and under raised floors, and no water pipes above racks where this can be avoidedSensors tested <Water sensor test frequency, for example every six months>
Heat and humidityCooling sized for the load, with monitoring that alerts above <Temperature alert threshold, for example 27 degrees Celsius>Alerts tested quarterly
Dust and spillsNo food or drink in equipment rooms, and the rooms kept cleanMonthly walk through by the site owner

4. Power and Cooling Supply

  1. All equipment runs through an uninterruptible power supply that lasts at least <UPS runtime at full load, for example 15 minutes>, long enough for a generator to start or for a clean shutdown.
  2. Backup power: <Generator arrangement, or none with a tested automatic shutdown>.
  3. Equipment with two power supplies is fed from two separate circuits.
  4. Power, cooling and network links are monitored, and alerts go to <Where power and cooling alerts go, for example the on call engineer>.
  5. The power supply and the shutdown or failover are tested at least once a year. A generator, where there is one, is run under load <Generator test frequency, for example monthly>. Every failed test is raised as an issue.

5. Cables

  1. Power and network cables run apart, in protected routes such as trunking or locked risers.
  2. Cables and patch panels are labelled, and the cable plan is kept current.
  3. Patch panels sit in locked racks. Network ports in public areas are turned off unless in use.

6. Where Equipment Is Placed

  1. Equipment sits in locked racks or rooms. Keys and codes are held by named people, and codes change when one of them leaves.
  2. Racks are kept away from windows, public view and water sources.
  3. Screens in equipment rooms face away from doors and windows.
  4. Visitors to equipment rooms are always escorted and signed in.

7. Servicing and Repairs

  1. Equipment and protections are serviced at the intervals the maker or the building sets, only by engineers on the approved list in <Where the approved engineer list is kept>.
  2. Engineers working in a secure area are supervised.
  3. Storage is removed or wiped before any equipment, laptops included, leaves for repair.
  4. Each fault and service visit is recorded with the date, the engineer, the work done and the result, on the equipment's record in Assets.
  5. After servicing, the site owner checks that the security settings and protections are back in place.

8. Wiping and Disposing of Equipment

  1. Before equipment is reused or disposed of, its storage is wiped with <Approved wiping method, for example cryptographic erase or an overwrite tool> or physically destroyed.
  2. A disposal provider issues a destruction record that lists each serial number.
  3. The asset is marked disposed in Assets, and the record is attached, under the Data Management Policy (control DM-16).

9. [Optional] Payment Devices

  1. Where {{company_name}} uses card terminals, ATMs or other payment devices, the site owner keeps a list of each device and its location.
  2. Devices are inspected for tampering or substitution <Payment device inspection frequency, set by risk>, and each inspection is recorded.
  3. Staff at those sites are trained to spot and report tampering.

10. Offices in Managed Buildings

Where a site is an office in a managed building, the site owner keeps the landlord's fire, power and maintenance certificates and checks each year that they are current, instead of repeating those tests.

Records and Evidence

RecordWhere it is kept in Verity
This standard and the site registerDocuments; attached as evidence to control PE-03
Hazard assessment and protections for each siteEvidence on PE-03, yearly
Service and fault records for site equipmentAssets, with a yearly summary attached to PE-03
Power, alarm and suppression test resultsEvidence on PE-03, yearly
Payment device list, inspection records and site staff trainingEvidence on PE-03, where payment devices are used
Destruction recordsEvidence on DM-16

Exceptions

A protection may be missing only while it is in the Risk register with an owner, a treatment and a date, and the executive sponsor has accepted the risk.

Review

The facilities or IT lead reviews this standard at least once a year, and after a new site opens, a site closes, or an environmental incident happens.

Related Documents

  • Physical Security Policy
  • Asset Management Policy
  • Data Management Policy
  • Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery Plan
  • Business Impact Analysis
